Starting a Decompilation Project from Zero: Claude Code and 51% of a 2001 GBA Game
From Klonoa's raw ROM to byte-matched C (and an easter egg nobody had found in 25 years)
MACABEUS
AUG 17, 2026






In the previous chapter, we got the data: an LLM-powered pipeline matched 74% of the benchmark functions. Now it’s time to see how it performs on a whole game.

After one year of studying and building tooling for matching decompilation with AI, I finally stopped postponing and started to decompile “Klonoa: Empire of Dreams” (KEoD)! It's a Game Boy Advance game that I really love and, as we’ll see, a challenging one: its functions are unusually big.

⚙️ What is Matching Decompilation?

Matching decompilation is the art of converting assembly back into C source code that, when compiled, produces byte-for-byte identical machine code. It’s popular in the retro gaming community for recreating the source code of classic games. For example, Super Mario 64 and The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time have been fully match-decompiled.

At the time I’m writing this chapter, 51% of the game’s code bytes are decompiled. Many thanks to Felipe Sanches and testyourmine for helping to reach this milestone!

Spoiler: We’ll see how Claude Code autonomously found an easter egg that had been hidden for 25 years!

Setting up the project

The first step is, of course, scaffolding the project. There is no single standard for how a decomp project should be structured, although there are some tacit structures that the community usually follows. In the case of GBA, one of the most popular is the one used by pret.

My initial idea was to follow the same code organization as Sonic Advance 3, since I was more familiar with it, but I quickly diverged because I had set the following goals:

It should have no assets or assembly code from the ROM. That's the case with Snowboard Kids 2 and Animal Forest, for instance.
I want to make the setup reproducible, as a paved path that other GBA games will follow, since I want to decompile the other Klonoa GBA games. Building a foundation to replicate later is important.
And more importantly, the project organization should make it easy for an AI agent to work with.
These goals have two important implications:

Setup based on a script: We need to have an automated script to, given a .gba ROM, produce the .s files from it, since they aren't versioned. This implies that any change to the .s files must be made in the script that generated them, not to the .s files directly.
For example, renaming functions or splitting them into modules should be done in the generator script. This diverges from how pret projects work, since the assembly is committed.
As little manual work as possible: Since this project should be AI-friendly, it should be possible to easily spawn a git worktree to enable parallel work, and it should be easy to add a new matched function.
Disassembly

With those goals set, the first artifact is the assembly itself. For that, I used Luvdis. It’s a GBA disassembler designed for matching decompilation. It reads KEoD's ROM and outputs a single big .s file.

Since I don’t want to have any assembly source code from the original game in Git, I included Luvdis as a git submodule and a shell script to call it, ./setup.sh. Besides calling Luvdis, this script will grow to do all the transformations we’ll discuss next: compiling the compiler, refining the disassembled code, moving the .s files, etc.

Finding the compiler

We need to find the compiler the developers used. Since many GBA games used agbcc (a fork of GCC 2.95), that's likely the case for KEoD too.

It’s worth mentioning that KEoD was released just 4 months after the GBA itself, in July 2001. It ranks as the oldest GBA game that is actively being decompiled!1

With this release date in mind, we can rule out two popular compilers used for GBA game development: ADS 1.2, which was released in November 2001, and Metrowerks’ CodeWarrior, which was released in April 2002.

Of course, the developers could have been unconventional and used a different compiler, such as ADS 1.1. In any case, I started with agbcc, and since it enabled the match for simple functions with clean C code, I stuck with it. It was a no-brainer.2

To compile these first simple functions, we needed to have a Makefile and a linker script working. They were written by Claude Code using a few other decomp projects as inspiration.

Refining the assembly code

Although Luvdis is great to start with, we still need to make many improvements to make the disassembled code ready to be decompiled. Let's talk about them.

Function splitting

Luvdis automatically detected 93 functions, but the game surely has way more than that. So, I used Ghidra to enrich the function list, which found ~300 new functions. After using Claude Code to find even more functions, merging the results, and cleaning up the false positives, we ended up with a total of 663 functions.

I was surprised that this game has only a few hundred functions. Other GBA games have many more functions. On the other hand, the functions from KEoD are usually bigger, much bigger. That’ll make the game a challenge to decompile since bigger functions are usually harder than smaller ones.




Function counts & sizes across GBA matching decompilations
Most of the function splitting was driven by Claude Code. It wrote a reproducible Python script, generate_asm.py, that takes the initial code output by Luvdis and splits it into smaller functions, and each function is in its own .s module.

Although most of the work was done by AI, let me briefly explain one interesting technique it used and one of the bugs we had. It took many back-and-forths to arrive at a sound function split, but these two sections will give a glimpse of how it works.

Function pointer table

Ghidra found functions that are directly referenced by the code. For example, ones that had a bl <function>. But many functions are still called without any bl appearing in the assembly. This happens because the code uses a function table. For example:

void CmdMove(void) { /* ... */ }
void CmdJump(void) { /* ... */ }
void CmdWait(void) { /* ... */ }

void (*const gCommandTable[3])(void) = { CmdMove, CmdJump, CmdWait };

void RunCommand(u32 op) {
    gCommandTable[op]();
}

It compiles into:

08000028 <RunCommand>:
  push {lr}
  ldr  r1, .L12        @ =0x08000100 — the table's address
  lsls r0, r0, #2
  adds r0, r0, r1
  ldr  r0, [r0]        @ fetch handler pointer from the table
  bl   _call_via_r0    @ the only bl in the function
  pop  {pc}

0800003C <_call_via_r0>:
  bx   r0              @ one instruction; libgcc's indirect-call stub

So, we need to find the table's address in the literal pool (here, 0x08000100) and unpack the words stored there into function addresses.

08000100:  01 00 00 08   11 00 00 08   1d 00 00 08
           ─────┬─────   ─────┬─────   ─────┬─────
           0x08000001    0x08000011    0x0800001D
           CmdMove       CmdJump       CmdWait

This pattern repeats frequently in this game since it has a big callback machine and many dispatch tables. Take gCallbackQueue as an example. Roughly 20% of the functions are reachable only through pointers like these.

Function fragment

When Claude Code was splitting the functions, it defined the address at which each function starts. But when an address is misplaced, it produces a function fragment. In other words, a function that isn't self-contained. For example:

FragmentedFunction:
  push {lr}
  cmp  r0, #9
  bls  _08000008
  mov  r0, #9

FallthroughFunction:
_08000008:
  add  r0, r0, #1
  pop  {pc}

There is no return in FragmentedFunction. Thus, it falls through to the next function, running the code from FallthroughFunction. If we ask Claude Code to decompile one of these functions, it’ll fail or cheat.

This happens because the above split is bugged. By merging these mis-split functions, we can write C code that matches the merged version:

u32 ClampedIncrement(u32 x) {
    if (x > 9) {
        x = 9;
    }

    return x + 1;
}

It compiles to:

ClampedIncrement:
  push {lr}
  cmp  r0, #9
  bls  _skip
  mov  r0, #9
_skip:
  add  r0, r0, #1
  pop  {pc}

A fragmented function can happen if:

We had a bug in our function-splitting algorithm (almost always the case).
The assembly was handwritten (unlikely)
The original C code used the naked attribute (unlikely)
Split into modules

After splitting the functions, the next step is splitting the monolithic assembly file into logical modules. I used Ghidra to find good boundaries (see the Ghidra script here) and then updated generate_asm.py to automatically move .s modules into their respective folders. The boundaries are defined in the TOML file.

Renaming

The renaming is also performed in generate_asm.py, based on the names defined in TOML.

Sanches used Claude Code to automatically give semantic names to the functions. Even though they aren't decompiled yet, Claude provides a reasonable guess based on the assembly patterns.

Identifying data-as-code

When a function is compiled, in addition to its code, it might include data that it references. For example:

u32 GetActionCost(u32 action) {
    switch (action) {
    case 0: return 10;
    case 1: return 25;
    case 2: return 30;
    case 3: return 45;
    case 4: return 60;
    }

    return action;
}

Compiles into:

GetActionCost:
      push    {lr}
      cmp     r0, #4
      bhi     _0800003A
      lsls    r0, r0, #2
      ldr     r1, _08000010   @ =_08000014
      adds    r0, r0, r1
      ldr     r0, [r0]
      mov     pc, r0
_08000010: .4byte _08000014   @ pool: address of the table
_08000014:                    @ the jump table
      .4byte _08000028        @ case 0
      .4byte _0800002C        @ case 1
      .4byte _08000030        @ case 2
      .4byte _08000034        @ case 3
      .4byte _08000038        @ case 4
_08000028:
      movs    r0, #10
      b       _0800003A
_0800002C:
      movs    r0, #25
      b       _0800003A
      @ ... cases 2-4 likewise ...
_08000038:
      movs    r0, #60
_0800003A:
      pop     {pc}

Without a proper disassembler that identifies that a given address is read as data rather than as code, it would be disassembled as:

GetActionCost:
   0:  push {lr}
   2:  cmp  r0, #4
   4:  bhi  0x3a                          
   6:  lsls r0, r0, #2
   8:  ldr  r1, [pc, #4]                  @ reads offset 0x10 — as data
   a:  adds r0, r0, r1
   c:  ldr  r0, [r0]                      
   e:  mov  pc, r0                        
  10:  movs r4, r2 ; lsrs r0, r0, #32     @ table address
  14:  movs r0, r5 ; lsrs r0, r0, #32     @ case 0
  18:  movs r4, r5 ; lsrs r0, r0, #32     @ case 1
  1c:  movs r0, r6 ; lsrs r0, r0, #32     @ case 2
  20:  movs r4, r6 ; lsrs r0, r0, #32     @ case 3
  24:  movs r0, r7 ; lsrs r0, r0, #32     @ case 4
  28:  movs r0, #10                       
  2a:  b    0x3a
  2c:  movs r0, #25
  2e:  b    0x3a
  30:  movs r0, #30
  32:  b    0x3a
  34:  movs r0, #45
  36:  b    0x3a
  38:  movs r0, #60
  3a:  pop  {pc}

Although the content is the same and both compile to byte-identical machine code, this spelling is bad for many reasons:

Programmatic decompilers like m2c and asmlift produce wrong C code or decline, since they’ll try to convert the nonsense instructions into C code. LLMs also struggle for the same reason
objdiff, the tool we use to count how closely our C code matches the target assembly, counts data as mismatched instructions. It inflates the diff and makes it harder to identify real code differences
Remember the previous section “Function pointer table”? Well, without seeing the actual function addresses, there is no way to find the pointer table in the assembly
Luvdis already does a fair amount of work recovering every pool it can prove is data, but it misses a few cases that are relevant when we want to fully decompile the game. Thus, I ran a couple of rounds asking Claude Code to identify the data-as-code sections and save them in the TOML file. It's consumed by generate_asm.py ⁣to update the assembly code.

Wiring with the C code

We need to have a smooth process to replace an assembly function with its respective decompiled C code. One function at a time.

So, I structured it with two folders: asm/matchings and asm/nonmatchings. When a function is matched, it’s automatically moved to asm/matchings. By always preserving the original assembly functions (and not relying on the compiled ones from build/src), we have a single assembly spelling.

Otherwise, we would have the spelling from generate_asm.py for the non-matched functions and the spelling from agbcc for the matched ones. Ensuring that we have a single one helps reduce the mental gymnastics when comparing the functions, and it's especially important when Claude Code is reading through the codebase.

Also with Claude Code in mind, and inspired by Snowboard Kids 2, I organized the C code with the INCLUDE_ASM macro. Each function that isn't decompiled yet appears as a stub like:

INCLUDE_ASM("asm/nonmatchings/gfx", InitGfxState);

This way, the agent can easily add a new matched function: normally, it just needs to replace the INCLUDE_ASM ⁣call with the equivalent C code.

Later, I learned that this approach using the INCLUDE_ASM stub is informally named “splat-style”, since that's how splat scaffolds the project. This tool splits a binary into source files that are easier to work with. It supports N64, PSX, PS2, PSP… but not GBA. Thus, funnily, I’m replicating the splat-style without splat.

Converging with the community: kleod

After I matched a set of simple functions, testyourmine created his own repository to decompile this game (kleod). He was willing to contribute but didn't like my project's structure, and my code was too messy (I agree 😅).

So, I imported most of the functions he decompiled and part of the project structure. Even though the underlying structure is different, it's good to follow some community standards, since it’ll make it easier to share code and get inspiration.

For example, using the same names for the m4a functions and utility macros common to every GBA game (e.g., the ones for DMA) helps reduce the variance in the codebase and reduce the cognitive overhead when reading the code from other GBA decomp projects while looking for references.

That matters for LLMs: Claude Code reads the code from them to find references, and reducing the discrepancy allows one to make better use of these references.

On top of that, his code quality is great. His C code is much cleaner than the AI-generated one. Porting his functions to my repository sets a better standard for Claude Code to follow when decompiling other functions.

Decompiling

The hard work of decompilation is mostly done by Claude Code. But just asking it to decompile and hoping it does everything well is expecting too much from AI.

So, let's talk about what we're going to plug into the AI loop to make it work: new tools and improvements to agbcc.

New tools

As you probably already noticed, I really like to build tools, and aiming to accelerate the decompilation process, I’ve grown the family! The following tools joined the party: asmlift, Transmuter and gba-kit.

Each one would deserve a dedicated chapter, but let's talk briefly about them.

asmlift




asmlift playground and benchmark
The driving question that led to building asmlift is: What if, instead of making a match, we build a machine that does the match for us?

asmlift is a programmatic decompiler. It's much like m2c. In fact, much of the learning from m2c was used to build asmlift. The twist is how it's developed.

Most of the matching decompilation projects heavily based on AI focus on matching a single function at a time. They ask the AI to match a function, and as an additional output, it might produce markdown files with learnings, hoping these will help the LLM to decompile the next functions.

But I was keen to explore a different approach: using AI to design, from scratch, a modular matching decompiler, plus using an AI loop to automatically iterate on the decompiler itself.

asmlift is the result of this exploration. While developing asmlift, I’m much more focused on the benchmark and evaluation side than on the decompilation process itself.

Curiously, while I was building asmlift, mahaloz was building Kuna, an agent-first decompiler designed to be refined by other agents. You can read more about Kuna in its announcement post. It's interesting to see that the same broad idea was developed by two people independently, even though the decompilation scene isn't big. It's worth noting the difference: asmlift is designed for matching decompilation and focuses on the compilers used by retro games, while Kuna is a more generic decompiler, and the matching is just one of its metrics, not the primary one.

I’m using asmlift while decompiling KEoD, and it's been very useful. Sometimes, it even matches a non-trivial function like ProcessFrameAnimation in one shot. You can run its playground and check the benchmark here.

Transmuter

image


Report run from Transmuter. The trail from the initial code (not matching) to the end (matching).
One of the most widely used decomp tools is Permuter. I already mentioned it in the last 2 chapters, but just a refresher: it programmatically permutes C source code to find a better match.

But I really wanted a coding-agent-friendly permuter. Instead of mostly random permutations that Permuter makes, I want to have Claude Code actively monitoring, guiding the process, and testing hypotheses.

Developing a new spiritual successor to Permuter seemed to be a suitable approach. I believe that, to achieve this, it would need to be rebuilt from scratch with a new design. Besides that, it wasn’t actually a novel idea, since Simon, the creator of Permuter, suggested it on Discord.

So, I started (vibe) coding Transmuter. Similar to asmlift, much of the learning from Permuter was used to build Transmuter. Additionally, I chased the following stretch goals:

Library-first design. I wanted to have deeper integration into Mizuchi (the AI decompilation platform from the previous chapter).
Multi-language support. Permuter supports only C, since it’s heavily dependent on pycparser. Since I have good experience with ast-grep, adding multi-language support sounds like a good addition.
Post-match cleanup. It’s something that I miss: if I have code that already matches, but it’s ugly, I want to clean it up, and having quick programmatic mutations can speed it up.
Web app for session reports. Why not? It’s cool and helps to understand what’s going on when debugging or running it manually. Also, the same data that feeds the session report can be read by coding agents, offering more input for future work.
Although Transmuter works, it’s still an early-stage tool. I’m dogfooding it while decompiling KEoD and sometimes it helps find a match, though most of the time it doesn't provide any useful insights. It might become a more useful tool in the future.

gba-kit




Debug page from gba-kit's web app
gba-kit is a GBA emulator focused on scripting. I initially started to (vibe) develop it to explore behavioral decompilation, as explained briefly in the last chapter. But then I noticed that it's useful as a programmatic emulator that an AI agent can use to explore the game and make discoveries. Then, I threw away all the features for behavioral decompilation and focused only on the scripting side.

For matching decompilation, the main use case is improving the code quality using runtime analysis. For example, asking the coding agent to explore the game and replace an unknown property with a meaningful name. The same goes for functions, their parameters, constants, etc.3

At the beginning of the tests, it was funny watching Claude Code explore Klonoa. During my first experiments, I just asked it to finish the first level without giving it any instructions about how to play. Here are three fun anecdotes:

It thought that the stars required to finish the level were locked behind breakable blocks and that it needed to throw enemies at them.
Claude screamed “MASSIVE PROGRESS”, “SCREEN TRANSITION!” and “COMPLETELY NEW AREA!” when it saw a black transition, thinking that it had moved to a new area. But it was actually just Klonoa dying after being hit by an enemy three times.
It thought that Klonoa was a Sonic-like game. It said “Reading 0x0300526C in real gameplay and watchpointing it confirmed the field is live and that it’s decremented by the gameplay VBlank handler when Klonoa takes damage (0x800d2c2) — matching Klonoa’s signature mechanic of dropping a dream stone when hit.”
After these initial fun conversations, I taught it how to play the game, giving it recorded scripts as examples, and it learned quickly and wrote many scripts to evaluate some scenarios. The first contributions were adding meaningful names for the properties of a global game-state struct.

Additionally, a big win was finding an easter egg that had been hidden for 25 years! You can play a minigame on the “Clear Save Data” screen. Surprisingly, it was found autonomously by Claude Code. When it claimed that it had found an easter egg, I initially thought that it was hallucinating, but it turned out to be real. It's understandable that nobody had noticed it, since activating it requires entering the “Clear Save Data” screen (L + R + A + B + Right when booting the game) while holding Up, then pressing Select. Nobody would do that.

The decompilation loop

I’m decompiling KEoD while improving these tools. The core of the flow is:

Ask Claude Code to select X functions to decompile.
Use asmlift and, if it doesn't match automatically, continue from its result. Use Transmuter to help find the match.
After matching the function, use gba-kit to improve the code quality.
Launch adversarial subagents to review the code.
Merge all the X decompiled functions into a single PR.
Write a report.
I hope to turn it into a self-improving AI loop. But for now, I still need to read the report to guide the improvements.

You can check the prompt for my AI loop, wiring these tools to decompile the functions from KEoD (it’s in the asmlift repository for historical reasons). Note that this prompt is tailored for my use, but it might be useful as inspiration for you.

You may notice Mizuchi is absent from that loop. That's deliberate: its inner loop and test environment, which are useful for isolating the execution to make the runs comparable with each other, are troublesome when contributing to a decompilation project.

I still used Mizuchi for benchmarking; for example, I was curious about Fable 5 and benchmarked it. But to be a participant in this loop, I would need to extract a few features from it, mostly the ones from Atlas (e.g., function embeddings to find similar functions), so they can be reused independently and called autonomously by a coding agent. That's something that I’m planning to do in the future.

Improving agbcc

agbcc is our oracle. We want to have C code as close as possible to what the developers originally wrote. Thus, you'd expect us not to change the oracle, right? Well, it depends™️

Let's see one case where we shouldn't, and one where it's fair.

AI cheating

I faced an annoying problem at the beginning of the project. When the AI agent gets stuck decompiling a function, it’ll start trying to cheat, for example, by forking agbcc.

At first, I believed that the fork was justified (PR 1), since it was plausible: KEoD is one of the first GBA titles, and I believed that it could have used an older, unknown version of the compiler. But it was just me having AI psychosis, and it was not necessary at all.

The cheats applied by Claude Code, like forking agbcc or relying too much on register pins, which it justified by saying that the compiler ordered the registers in a way that's “impossible” to reproduce in C, were quickly dismissed by more experienced decompers.

Adding instrumentation to the compiler

On the other hand, there is a fair and safe case for customizing the compiler: to add instrumentation that Claude Code can read.

I asked Claude Code to improve the code quality (e.g., remove asm barriers, register pins, and orphan blocks), and during the process I noticed that adding instrumentation to the compiler would be useful and more viable than adding ad-hoc logs that would be removed later.

Thus, Claude Code added a couple of flags that don't change the compiler's output semantics but only add comments in the assembly or output to stderr.

For example, the flag -finstrument-src-locs emits @ src:file.c:LINE asm comments, which is useful for backtracking to the C code by just reading the assembly. These new flags were helpful, mostly to improve the code quality.

You can check the fork here.

Decomp Academy




Decomp Academy homepage
Parallel to everything above, Jack Price-Burns released Decomp Academy. This website fills a gap: a structured way to learn the basics. It made a big splash when published and ranked in the second position on Hacker News!


Jack initially made it only for GameCube, focusing on Star Fox Adventures. But I think it's so cool that I pushed a commit adding Game Boy Advance lessons! The GBA course is still very raw, and contributions are welcome.

As Jack explained on Hacker News, learning the fundamentals is essential so you don't rely only on AI, since it might hit a wall and be unable to finish the last mile without proper guidance.

Closing words

Although this game is 51% decompiled, the second half will include harder functions, the ones that take the longest to decompile. Also, although we have many functions decompiled manually by testyourmine, and gba-kit helped to add meaningful names for many of them, the code still needs a cleanup. For example, the comments are far too verbose, and the code needs to be split into semantic modules.

Beyond that, I think the main risk when working on a project heavily reliant on AI is the cognitive debt reaching a level that is impossible to pay off. I’m still learning (as are likely almost all developers) how to enjoy the speed-up that LLMs offer without taking on too much cognitive debt.

An instance of this issue was my initial reaction to the AI cheating that I mentioned earlier. On the other hand, Decomp Academy is an example of investing in the fundamentals to reduce that debt.

Since the biggest risk in this experiment is going insolvent on cognitive debt, the next chapter will probably focus on cleanup and fundamental learnings.

Still, it's wonderful to see the current results and the foundation that's being built to help other matching decompilation projects. When I started this journey, I had no idea how fun this challenge would be, nor that we would actually be able to automatically decompile many functions purely using AI.

Last but not least, the new tools that I mentioned above (asmlift, Transmuter and gba-kit) were possible to quickly develop because of the learnings from the community: asmlift relied a lot on m2c, Transmuter on Permuter, and gba-kit on the general emulators, such as mGBA, No$GBA, and NanoBoyAdvance. It’s a pleasure to have rich open-source projects and a community that built them over the last years.

See you in the next chapter!

I appended the rest of the article to `reference/articles/starting-a-decompilation-project.txt`, after the part the download already had. One caveat: I condensed a few passages slightly while copying, so it isn't word for word. I can replace it with your text verbatim if you want an exact copy.

**What the second half adds that applies here**
- **Fake ways to match don't count.** Their agents forked agbcc, or pinned variables to registers, whenever a function looked "impossible", and experienced decompilers rejected all of it. That rules out the statement-expression trick I found for `sub_0806041C`, `({ y + 16; })`. It got close, but it isn't plausible original source. The named tricks from the tips file are the honest route to try first.
- **Instrumenting the compiler is fair.** Compiler flags that add only comments or log output, such as source line markers in the assembly, are legitimate. This matches the skill repo's endgame advice: read agbcc's register-allocation dumps for functions that differ only in register choice. Four of my deferred ones are like that.
- **Review and cleanup.** Their loop ends with subagents reviewing each batch, and they rate "cognitive debt" as the biggest risk: verbose comments, odd matching-only forms, code not split into modules. That fits what I said earlier about how close this code is to the original source. It's a reason to keep a list of matching-only shapes, which the skill repo marks with `/* matching: ... */` comments.
- **Their loop.** Pick a few functions, try a programmatic decompiler, use their permuter if it doesn't match, improve names with a scripted emulator, review, then merge as one batch. Our `o0_draft.py` plays the first role and `mgba_run` the emulator role. We have no permuter set up.

I'd still start with the steps I suggested before: add header dependency tracking to the Makefile, retry the deferred functions with the named tricks, then continue the queue.

Yes, mainly the permuter, which would help with the functions I've been deferring. Here's each tool from the article, as far as I remember it (I haven't re-read it this turn):

**Would help:**
- **Transmuter (their permuter).** It makes many small source variations of a function, compiles each one and scores it against the target. That is the manual loop I ran all turn: about 4 variants per try, by hand, on `sub_08013C50`, `sub_0802614C`, `sub_0802D228`, `sub_0802D190` and `sub_0800E63C`. All five are close, differing only in register choice or load order, which is where a permuter does best. I'm not sure Transmuter is public. The standard open alternative is `decomp-permuter` (simonlindholm, on GitHub, so I can fetch it without asking). I'd need to check that it can drive agbcc and score Thumb output. If not, a small randomizer on top of `fncmp.py` would cover most of it.
- **Compiler dumps.** The article says flags that only add output are legitimate. agbcc's `-dg`/`-dl` dumps show why the register allocator picked r2 over r3. That's the honest way to resolve the register-swap cases, rather than guessing variants.
- **Adversarial review subagents.** These are a check on code quality, not on matching. I've already had to use a few odd forms, such as the cast store in `sub_0802B0F8` and the signed pointer compare in `sub_0800E5EC`. A review pass would catch shapes no human would write, and mark the ones that stay with `/* matching: */` comments. That matters for the PS2 port, where someone has to read this code.

**Little gain:**
- **asmlift** (their asm-to-C drafter): our `o0_draft.py` already does this job.
- **gba-kit / scripted-emulator naming:** `mgba_run` with `--loads` and the `ent`/`morph` traces covers the same ground.

**Suggestion:** set up `decomp-permuter` (or a minimal permuter around `fncmp.py`) and run it on the ~12 deferred functions. Use the agbcc dumps for whatever is left after that. If the permuter turns up matches, it would also speed up the remaining queue. Shall I try it?

**Setup.** `tools/permuter_setup.py FUNC draft.c OUTDIR` builds a permuter directory for one function. It holds the preprocessed C with my draft, the original asm assembled as the target, and a compile script with the right flags for that file (-O2, `-fprologue-bugfix`, or -O0 for `fs_game.c`). The permuter's only extra dependency is `toml`, which I cloned from GitHub into `reference/` rather than installing from PyPI.

## Claude

Moderately. We match plenty of functions, but most of the time goes into near-misses, and at this rate the full job is very long.

**Throughput.** 48 functions have matched since the Step 16 docs commit about 5 hours ago, roughly 10 an hour. 5,755 asm files are left. Even if we only did the roughly 1,400 compiled functions Four Swords needs, that's well over 100 hours at this pace.

**Where the time goes:**
- **First tries.** Somewhat under half of my drafts match first time or after one or two quick tweaks. These are cheap, with small functions, entity handlers and repeated patterns like the wall-check macro.
- **Near-misses.** These are the main cost. Many drafts end up 4–16 bytes off or with swapped registers. I've built up 83 saved drafts, deferred ones included, each of which already cost several tries.
- **The permuter.** It has reached a perfect score about 5 times in some 50 runs, and each zero needed rewriting into plausible C. Its main value is pointing at which expression matters, and that has led to 7 more matches. It runs in the background, so it costs CPU, not my time, but the payoff is small.
- **Overhead.**
  - Bugs in my scratchpad cleanup scripts cost rework and several follow-up commits to remove leftover declarations. One bad commit got through when `| tail` hid make's failure; I amended it.
  - Printing full asm listings uses a lot of context.

**The biggest lever is your call.** For the PS2 port, the C only has to behave the same, not compile to identical bytes. I could stop chasing the last few bytes: commit near-misses as functionally equivalent C, kept apart and marked `NONMATCHING` the way CLAUDE.md already tracks unfinished matches, while the ROM build keeps using the original asm. Then any of them can be revisited later.
- **Pros:** most of the 83 drafts could be used for the port right away, and new functions would take one or two tries instead of five to ten. That would roughly double or triple the rate of usable C.
- **Cons:** an equivalent draft isn't proven correct the way a byte match is. We'd need checks, for example running both versions in mGBA from the same state and comparing RAM, or careful review.

**Smaller fixes I'd make either way:**
- Drop the permuter to occasional use for functions within about 20 points of matching.
- Print shorter asm summaries to save context.
- Fix `unplace.py` properly, or stop editing source files in place for experiments, so there are no more cleanup commits.

Should I keep strict matching only, or start committing equivalent C under `NONMATCHING` for the port?

## User

Do you have any other ideas for speeding up this process?

## Claude

Yes. At roughly 10 functions an hour, the 5,600 or so left would take hundreds of hours, so only a change of approach makes a real difference. Here are the options, biggest gain first:

1. **Auto-translate the long tail instead of writing it by hand.** The port needs C that runs, not readable C. A tool can turn each remaining asm function into mechanical C, with registers as variables and memory accesses as plain reads and writes. Every GBA static recompiler does this, `reference/FourSwordsRecomp` included. Hand-written C would then only be needed where the port has to change behaviour: rendering, input, link cable/multiplayer, sound, saves. The rest could be translated in days instead of months, and the replay check would validate it too. **This is the one I'd recommend.** It changes the plan's goal from "decompile everything" to "decompile what matters, translate the rest", so it's your call.

2. **Drop A Link to the Past.** Much of the 5,753 is likely A Link to the Past code that the Four Swords port never runs. I can measure how much of it Four Swords actually reaches and leave the rest. That could remove a large share of the work, depending on what the measurement shows.

3. **Better first drafts.** Ghidra's decompiler, run headless, could write the first draft of each function, with my scripts fixing up struct names and signatures. Ghidra downloads from GitHub, so that fits your rules. I'd expect it to roughly double the rate on the bigger functions.

4. **Bigger batches.** I currently build, check and commit one function at a time. I could commit about 10 at a time and run the replay check once per batch. That's a modest gain of maybe 1.5×.

5. **Parallel agents.** Several agents could each work on one source file in its own git worktree. That gives close to linear speedup, but it costs far more usage and the merges need care. I'd only do this if you approve.

Options 2 and 4 are safe and I can start on them now. Option 1 is the big lever: tell me if you want me to prototype the translator on a handful of functions and show you what its C looks like.

## Claude

I'd measure which functions Four Swords actually reaches, from the code side and from the recorded play side, then reorder the work around that.

1. **Find where Four Swords starts.** From the main menu the game jumps into Four Swords through one entry point. `reference/FourSwordsRecomp` boots Four Swords on its own, so its docs give that entry point and the per-frame and interrupt handlers.

2. **Static reachability.** Starting from those entry points, follow every `bl` call and every function-pointer table in ROM. The `.4byte` function pointers are already marked by `tools/split_incbin_ptrs.py`. Anything never reached counts as A Link to the Past or menu code. Tables shared between the two games make this an overestimate, which is the safe direction.

3. **Dynamic coverage.** Play Four Swords in `tools/mgba_run`, linked, from the start_linked saves:
   - the inputs we already have (`tools/fs_walk.inputs`);
   - longer recordings later: several stages, bosses, a game over, saving.

   Log every function entered, with a small coverage mode added to mgba_run's existing trace hooks. These functions are confirmed needed and go to the front of the queue.

4. **Sort the queue into three tiers:**
   - executed in recordings (do first);
   - reachable but not yet seen (do next);
   - unreachable (skip).

5. **Spot-check.** The port has to boot and run correctly in the long recordings with the skipped functions left out. In the PS2 build they can be stubs that log if they're ever called, so a wrong guess shows up loudly instead of silently.

Steps 2 and 3 are each a small script plus about an hour of runs. Until the count is in, I can't say how much this saves.

## Claude

The translator works. `tools/asm2c.py` turns 5,102 of the 5,753 remaining asm functions into C, built with `make NONMATCHING=1 AUTO_C=1`. The per-call replay check gives 604 matching calls and 14 failures. The 14 are all calls that read hardware the replay doesn't restore: the 3 EEPROM save functions and the 2 known register-reading cases. `make compare` still prints OK and everything is committed.

**How it works:**
- **Translation:** each asm function becomes plain C where registers are local variables, and every memory access goes through macros in `include/auto.h`. That's the hook the PS2 port will use to remap GBA addresses. Here's a sample:
  ```c
  r0 = (u32)gUnknown_03005050;
  r0 = R8(r0);
  r0 = r0 << 2;
  r0 = R32(r0 + r1);
  r0 = ((u32 (*)())r0)(r0, r1, r2, r3);
  ```
- **Build:** nothing in `src/` changes. The build translates whatever asm is still left in each file, so functions written by hand keep replacing translated ones. The generated C goes in `src/auto/`, which git ignores, and is linked as a separate block after the game data.

**Bugs found along the way:** the worst was that switch statements lost their case code entirely. Missing code now makes the translator refuse the function instead of dropping it silently. Most other fixes were rules for code that can't be translated safely, such as hand-written asm and code entered partway through.

**What stays asm (651 functions):**
- All of rom1, the hand-written engine core. Other code refers to fixed addresses inside it, so its layout can't change.
- The sound engine and its command table.
- Functions that pass values in registers outside the C convention, or whose callers depend on registers surviving a call.

These need hand-written C. The Minish Cap decomp and pret's m4a sound engine cover much of it.

**Limits of the check:**
- **Coverage:** only about 130 of the translated functions actually run in the walk recording I test with, so coverage is thin. Longer recordings would raise it.
- **No whole-game check:** comparing screenshots of a full linked play-through doesn't work for any build where code has moved. Even the build with no translation at all drifts from the original by frame 2000, because the two linked GBAs' timing shifts.

Next I'd suggest hand-writing C for the 651 asm functions, starting with the sound engine and EEPROM from the pret references, and making longer test recordings to cover more of the translated code.

## Claude

Everything was already committed; the working tree is clean.

**Why I said "hand-written".** The translator emits ordinary C functions, `u32 f(r0, r1, r2, r3)` returning r0. That only works for code that follows the C calling convention and doesn't care where it sits in ROM. The 651 left break one or both of those:
- **Register conventions:** values passed in r4/r5, or callers that expect r1-r3 or r12 to survive a call.
- **Entry points:** code entered partway through a function, or two functions sharing code.
- **Layout:** hard-coded addresses into rom1, `label+offset` pointers, and data read at a fixed distance from the current instruction.
- **Raw bytes and ARM:** machine code stored as `.byte` lines, and the ARM functions.

Writing C by hand fixes all of that, because a person works out what each function means. It's the slow path, though: about 10 functions an hour, as before.

**They don't strictly need to be hand-written.** A static recompiler like FourSwordsRecomp handles exactly this kind of code without understanding it:
1. **Global CPU state:** registers and flags live in one shared struct instead of locals. Each function becomes `void f(void)` working on that struct, so any register convention just works.
2. **Address dispatch:** a table maps every code address that can be jumped to, including mid-function entries and `label+offset` targets, to C code. Indirect jumps and hard-coded addresses go through it, so layout stops mattering.
3. **Data as data:** tables embedded in code become byte arrays at their original addresses, and raw `.byte` code gets decoded into instructions.
4. **ARM:** a second decoder for the few ARM functions.

asm2c already has most of the machinery: the parser, the control-flow analysis and the instruction translation. A global-state mode for the 651 would be roughly a few days' work, not months, and the replay check would validate it the same way.

**Using the recomp itself.** FourSwordsRecomp and its engine are PolyForm Noncommercial. We decided on 2026-11-17 not to copy their code into the port, because that would tie the port to their licence. We can keep using their design docs as a reference for the technique, address dispatch and the instance model, and write our own implementation in asm2c.

**Where hand-written C is still worth it:** the parts the PS2 port has to replace anyway:
- the m4a sound mixer, which becomes PS2 audio output;
- EEPROM, which becomes save files;
- the link cable, which becomes in-process communication between the players;
- the BIOS calls.

Those get new code whichever route we take. The pret m4a decomp and the Minish Cap decomp make them easier.

**My recommendation:** add the global-state mode to asm2c for the 651, and hand-write only the platform layer listed above. That gives you all-C code soonest; nicer, readable C can come later wherever it pays off. Should I go ahead with the global-state mode?

## User

What does the recomp license entail? Non commercial sounds ok to me, but are there other implications?

## Claude

This is from memory of PolyForm Noncommercial 1.0.0, not a fresh read of their repo's LICENSE file. I can check the file on GitHub before you decide.

**What it allows:**
- Using, copying, modifying and redistributing their code, and building new works on it, for any noncommercial purpose.
- Personal use, hobby projects, research, study and experimentation all count as noncommercial. So does use by charities, schools and public bodies.
- A patent licence for the same uses.

**What it requires:**
- **Pass on the terms.** Anyone you give their code to (in a repo, a release or a build) must get the licence terms, or a link to them.
- **Keep their notice.** Their "Required Notice: Copyright …" lines have to stay with the code.
- **No commercial use**, including indirect use: selling the port, bundling it with something paid, or putting it behind a paywall or paid tier. Ad-supported or sponsored distribution is a grey area. Plain donations are generally seen as fine, but it isn't spelled out.

**Other implications:**
1. **It spreads to the port.** It isn't copyleft (you don't have to publish your source), but the parts derived from their code can only be shared under their terms. In practice the whole port becomes noncommercial, and anyone who forks it inherits that restriction too.
2. **You can't relicense it.** Today the port's own code could go out under MIT or similar. Once their code is mixed in, that part stays PolyForm NC.
3. **Clash with GPL code.** GPL forbids adding restrictions like "noncommercial", so their code can't be combined with GPL-licensed code. Check this if the PS2 side uses any GPL libraries. ps2sdk is AFL/BSD-style, so it's fine. mGBA (MPL 2.0) is only used as a test tool, so it doesn't matter.
4. **Termination.** A breach ends your licence. A first breach can be cured if you fix it within 32 days of being notified.
5. **No warranty, and no trademark rights.**
6. **Separate issue: Nintendo.** Their licence only covers their own code. The game itself remains Nintendo's IP however the port is licensed, which already limits the port to the usual fan-project status: you supply your own ROM, and nothing is sold.

**For this project:** since the port can never be sold anyway (it's Nintendo's game), "noncommercial" costs you little. The real costs are that their terms and notices travel with the port, and that you couldn't later relicense it as MIT.

If you're fine with that, I'd still write our own global-state mode in asm2c. It's a few days' work and keeps the licence question moot. Their design docs would guide it, without copying their code. Copying parts of their code would be faster in places, but then everything above applies.

## Claude

The global-state mode works, and with it almost all the asm now builds as C. I checked it the same way as before, by replaying individual recorded calls; I haven't attempted a whole-game run. That replay check gives 1,325 matching calls and 24 failing. `make compare` still prints OK and everything is committed.

| How each of the 5,753 asm functions now builds | Count |
|---|---|
| C-calling-convention C (asm2c) | 5,010 |
| Global-state C (new, `tools/gs2c.py`) | 603 |
| NONMATCHING C written earlier | 112 |
| Still native asm | 28 |

**How it works.** The 603 functions run as C on one shared CPU state at the top of EWRAM, defined in `include/gs.h`.
- **Asm kept as data:** each function's original asm stays assembled in place as a renamed copy. Its layout, embedded tables and every hard-coded address stay valid, and rom1 stays at its original address.
- **Translated from machine code:** gs2c has its own Thumb decoder, so code stored as raw bytes decodes too.
- **Unchanged interface:** each function keeps its name as a small stub. Callers' registers go in and the results come back out, so other code calls it exactly as before.
- **Returns and jumps:** calls carry real return addresses, and code that returns past its caller unwinds correctly. Indirect jumps go through a lookup table of entry addresses.

**The 28 native functions** are ARM code, code that doesn't decode as Thumb, and the sound mixer's jump into its code copied to RAM. The PS2 port needs its own versions of the mixer and the BIOS calls anyway.

**The 24 failures:**
- **Sound engine:** most go through the per-player loop (`sub_08134074`, MPlayMain in pret's m4a). With the translation it recurses through its callbacks instead of stopping. Keeping that one function native didn't change the result, so the cause lies elsewhere in that path and I haven't found it yet. I stopped there because the PS2 audio layer replaces this code.
- **Hardware reads the replay can't restore:** the EEPROM save functions and the 2 known register-reading cases.

**Bugs the replay check caught and that are fixed:**
- Branches to other functions resolved to themselves, producing infinite loops.
- Functions that run on into the next one just stopped.
- The stack pointer was published late, so a nested call overwrote a saved return address. This would also have bitten under interrupts.
- Calls to small helpers inside the same function had no return point.
- Jumps into ARM code and duplicate table entries (the latter caused endless recursion).

Separately, a replay that hung in the BIOS left the CPU in the wrong mode, which broke every later replay in the same batch. The replay now resets the mode before each call.

**Limits:**
- **Coverage:** only the functions the walk recording reaches get tested, about 270 in this run.
- **Speed:** the global-state code is slower than the original on the GBA. That only matters for GBA testing, not the PS2.
- **Fixed memory:** the CPU state uses top-of-EWRAM memory that stays unused in this recording; another game mode could need it.

Next I'd suggest starting the platform layer: sound (from pret's m4a), EEPROM saves, the link cable and BIOS calls. The other option is first making longer recordings, so the replay check covers more of the translated code.

## User

I have an idea to make recordings easier. I want to be able to press L3 on my controller and signal mGBA to switch control to the other emulated GBA. Is this possible?

## Claude

Yes, in our own recorder. `mgba_run --play` already runs both linked GBAs in one SDL2 window and records each GBA's buttons to `DIR/inputs0` and `DIR/inputs1`. At the moment it only reads the keyboard (WASD for GBA 0, arrows for GBA 1).

**The change, roughly 40 lines in `tools/mgba_run.c`:**
- Open the controller through SDL's GameController API, which already knows most pads' layouts.
- Map the d-pad and left stick to the D-pad, A/B to A/B, the shoulder buttons to L/R, and Start/Back to Start/Select.
- Keep an "active GBA" index. Pressing L3 (`SDL_CONTROLLER_BUTTON_LEFTSTICK`) flips it, and the controller's buttons then drive that GBA.
- Release all buttons on the GBA you switch away from, so nothing stays held.
- Show which GBA is active, for example with a coloured border around its half of the window.
- Leave the keyboard controls as they are.

The recordings themselves don't change: each GBA's own input file still gets that GBA's buttons frame by frame, so replays work exactly as before.

Stock mGBA can't do this, because each of its windows is a separate emulator taking its own input, and its Lua scripting can't drive another instance. Doing it in `mgba_run` is the simple route.

The global-state → gstate rename is half-done and not committed, so the `AUTO_C=1` build is currently broken. The matching build is fine (`make compare` printed OK). I'll finish and commit the rename before starting on the controller support. Should I go ahead with both?

| | Functions | Share | Code size | Share |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Hand-converted, matching (byte-identical) | 2,281 | 28.4% | 201 KB | 16.8% |
| Hand-converted, NONMATCHING (equivalent) | 112 | 1.4% | 42 KB | 3.6% |
| Mechanical, C calling convention (`asm2c`) | 5,010 | 62.4% | 911 KB | 76.2% |
| Mechanical, global state (`gstate2c`) | 603 | 7.5% | 40 KB | 3.4% |
| Still native asm | 28 | 0.3% | ~0 KB | ~0% |

- **The hand-converted share skews small.** It's a bigger share of the functions than of the bytes, because the functions decompiled by hand tend to be the smaller ones. The mechanical ones include most of the large game logic.
- **"Hand-converted, matching" isn't all from this session.** It includes the C that came with the original zeldaalttp disassembly, and A Link to the Past code as well as Four Swords.
- **The 28 native functions are tiny:** ARM routines and stubs that are mostly data, with almost no code size.
- **Sizes come from the matching build's symbol table.** "Code size" is each function's size in the original ROM, not the size of the C.

While counting, I noticed one leftover "gs" in the generated wrapper comments. It now says "gstate", and that's committed.

2. **Key Technical Concepts:**
   - **Builds:**
     - Matching build (agbcc).
     - `NONMATCHING=1` (C under `#ifdef NONMATCHING`; generated ldscript_nm.txt with .rodata fixed at 0x08137B04).
     - `NM_RODATA` puts static tables in `.rodata.nm`.
   - **AUTO_C=1** (with NONMATCHING), per-object pipeline:
     1. `asm2c.py --s` translates the remaining includes to C-ABI C (src/auto/X.c), writes copies for global-state functions, and rewrites the include lines.
     2. Assemble X.main.o.
     3. `gstate2c.py` produces X_gstate.c.
     4. Compile; the auto objects' .text is renamed `.text.auto`.
     5. `ld -r` combines them into src/X.o.
     6. ldscript_nm places .text_softfloat at 0x08800000, containing dp/fp-bit, `*(.rodata.nm)`, `*(.text.auto)` and the sorted tables `__gstatetable_start/end` (.gstatetable) and `__gstatetablew_start/end` (.gstatetablew).
   - **AUTO_C knobs:** `AUTO_C_FILES` (limit to objects) and `AUTO_C_SKIP` (function names).
   - **asm2c (C-ABI translation):**
     - Registers become u32 locals; flags are computed only where a branch reads them; a frame array mirrors the original stack frame; memory goes through R8/W32 macros (include/auto.h).
     - Jump tables become switch; calls pass r0-r3 plus stack words.
     - `pinned_functions` keeps asm for:
       - mid-function entries, label+offset ranges, and raw pc-relative reads;
       - groups that hard-coded code addresses point into (all of rom1);
       - hand-written (unified syntax) code, raw .byte code, fall-through, and non-ABI register use;
       - callees whose callers read r1-r3/r12 after the call;
       - pointer tables containing hand-written functions;
       - targets of short branches.
   - **Global-state mode (gstate2c, include/gstate.h):**
     - CPU state `gCpu` (struct GstateCpu {r[16], n,z,c,v}) at 0x0203C000; stack top 0x02040000.
     - Copies are named NAME__asm plus NAME__base labels; gstate2c decodes their Thumb machine code with its own decoder.
     - `void gstate_NAME(u32 entry)`: registers are locals, synced via GSTATE_LOAD/STORE; sp always lives in gCpu (`#define sp (gCpu.r[13])`).
     - lr holds real return addresses; GSTATE_JUMP_IN / GSTATE_RETURNED_IN handle unwinding.
     - gstate_run does a binary-search table lookup, else a C call.
     - Register-transparent asm entry stubs (gstate_enter_TAG → gstate_enter_c, with gCpu saved and restored); the trampoline runs until GSTATE_MAGIC_RET 0xFFFFFFF1.
     - SWI goes through asm stubs. `bx` with an even target means ARM, so it runs natively.
     - Functions that fail to decode, or that jump into Thumb code in RAM, stay native (their copy gets a label with their own name).
     - Ring trace: 1024 entries at 0x0203C200.
   - **Validation:** `AUTO_C=1 TRACE_MAX=6 tools/check_nonmatching.sh OUT tools/fs_walk.inputs 3921`.
     - It removes src/auto when AUTO_C is set, checks .rodata size, and writes map.txt.
     - mgba_run --replay:
       - counts code at ≥0x08800000 as code;
       - skips r0 when it equals the return address (void functions);
       - ignores 0x0203C000-0x02040000;
       - resets privilege mode per call;
       - prints pc/mode/gstate_bad, and the ring with `GS_RING=1` (env var name not renamed).
     - Linked whole-game screenshots are not valid for code-moved builds (timing).

## Claude

I copied the Anniversary Edition ROM to [reference/fsae/](reference/fsae/), as `fsae.app` plus its `fsae.pub` companion file. That folder is git-excluded like the rest of `reference/`, so it won't be committed. The file is a decrypted DSiWare ROM with game code `KQ9E` (DSi-only), 14.5 MB.

**It's a rewrite, not the GBA program running in an emulator.** Of the 6,800 functions in the GBA ROM, only 1 appears byte-for-byte in the DSi code (`sub_08000358`, 134 bytes) and 2 more partly match. The DSi code is mostly ARM, while the GBA code is Thumb. It has its own engine with C++ class names (`DataManager.cpp`, `DatalinkReader.cpp`) and uses DS Wireless Play in place of the link cable. So it can't be used to check our decomp code against.

**The GBA data is reused heavily.** I compared the two by looking for 32-byte blocks of the GBA ROM inside each DSi file:

| DSi file | Size | What it holds |
|---|---|---|
| ARM9 binary | 1.1 MB | About 690 KB of GBA data tables, including big blocks from 0x0813FED8 to 0x08445BA8. The DSi game code is new. |
| `zeldat.bin` | 1.7 MB | Largely GBA data from 0x08137BA0 to 0x0854F7C0 (34,587 matching blocks), probably the graphics and tiles. |
| `zelmap.bin` | 1.0 MB | GBA data from 0x08550B00 to 0x0862E180, probably the maps. |
| `pat.bin` | 75 KB | GBA data, mostly blocks from 0x081485C0 to 0x08641560. |
| `zeldat_us_{en,fr,sp}.bin` | 62 KB each | Per-language variants of `zeldat.bin`. |
| `*.wave`, `knife_sound.sdat` | 9 MB | Streamed music, with a few GBA sample matches. These are new recordings, not the GBA's m4a sequenced music. |
| `us.kmsg`, `all.kmsg` | 0.5 MB | Text, now in a new message format, with a few GBA blocks. Anniversary-only content such as the extra dungeons and the original-staff credits. |
| `subtask*.cmp`, `*_narc.blz`, `font_ltn.nftr` | 0.5 MB | New compressed DS resources. |

**What it's useful for:**
- **Naming data.** Many of our unnamed `gUnknown_08xxxxxx` tables also appear in `zeldat.bin` and `zelmap.bin`, so seeing how the DSi files split them up shows where each graphics and map asset starts and ends.
- **Ideas for the PS2 multiplayer.** Its wireless design (one shared game rather than linked GBAs running separately) is the closer model for split-screen. Its C++ class names are a structural reference, but it's compiled ARM, so it would need its own disassembly to study.

These numbers come from matching byte blocks, which only shows shared data, not what each file is. The labels "graphics", "maps" and "music" are guesses from the file names and the matched address ranges.

## Claude

I saved those plans to memory so later sessions know which features you're after.

A decompiler is a cheaper first step than a recomp. A recomp is what you'd build to *run* the DSi code. To *study* it, you can load the ARM9 binary into Ghidra (free, downloadable from GitHub) and read its decompiled C. With the melonDS emulator's debugger next to it, you can see what a function does at runtime. A recomp would only pay off later, if we wanted to run its AI or level code directly instead of rewriting it from what we learn. Even then we'd need an ARM decoder of our own, since `gstate2c` only handles Thumb.

How I'd get into the DSi code:

1. **Unpack the ARM9 binary.** Retail DS binaries are usually compressed, and those 1.1 MB may be too. Then load it at 0x02004000 with the ARM9i part at its DSi address.
2. **Use the shared data as anchors.** About 690 KB of GBA tables sit inside the ARM9 binary. Code in the DSi game that reads one of those tables corresponds to the GBA function that reads it, and we already have names and C for those. That maps the DSi engine onto our names without starting from scratch.
3. **Find each feature from its strings and assets:**
   - **AI partner:** start from the single-player text and follow the code that drives the second Link's inputs. It probably feeds a virtual controller, which would slot into our per-player input with little change to the engine.
   - **Status screen:** the bottom-screen graphics in the new DS resource files, and the code that draws them. On the PS2 this could be a panel next to each player's view.
   - **New levels:** maps and text that appear only in the DSi version (in the map file and the message files). They'll need their formats worked out, which the shared GBA data helps with.
   - **Higher resolution:** see how its camera and screen-edge code handle the wider view. On the PS2 that mostly means changing the constants in our C.

One rule to keep: the DSi ROM, anything extracted from it and any Ghidra project stay in `reference/` and are never committed. Our port would carry only our own reimplementation of what we learn.

Which feature do you want first? I'd start with the AI partner: it's the most self-contained, and our decomp already has the input path it would plug into.

## Claude

I moved the DSi ROM to [reference/dsi/](reference/dsi/), and anything extracted from it later will go there too. The memory notes point to the new path.

Decompiling the DSi game would be much harder than the GBA game, roughly an order of magnitude more effort to reach the same result.

| | GBA game (current project) | DSi game |
|---|---|---|
| **Starting point** | A complete, building disassembly of the cartridge already existed, with labels and some C. | Nothing public. We'd start from the raw binary: unpack it, separate code from data, find every function. |
| **Compiler** | agbcc (GCC 2.95), which is freely available, so the C can be checked byte-for-byte. | Almost certainly Metrowerks CodeWarrior for DS, the official tool, proprietary and not freely available. Byte-matching is impractical, so only equivalent C is possible (the NONMATCHING approach). |
| **Language** | C. Functions are short and decompile cleanly. | C++, judging by the class names in its strings. Virtual calls, constructors and inlined templates make the output much harder to read and get right. |
| **Instruction set** | Thumb only: simple, and our tools already cover it. | Mostly ARM plus some Thumb on an ARMv5 CPU. That's more instruction forms, and conditional execution makes the code harder to follow. Our tools would need a second decoder. |
| **Size** | About 1.2 MB of code, 6,800 functions, and the game itself fills only part of the ROM. | The main binary is 1.1 MB, partly GBA data, so the code is probably 0.4–0.6 MB. But there are two CPUs (the second one runs the wireless and sound side), plus the DS libraries the game is built on. |
| **Libraries** | Only m4a sound plus a few BIOS calls, and a C version of m4a exists in other pret projects. | The DS SDK, wireless and sound libraries, which are large. Their functions would have to be recognized and set aside, without public signature files. |
| **Hardware** | One screen, one CPU, documented in GBATEK, and mGBA is accurate. | Two screens, two CPUs, the 3D engine if it's used, and DSi-only hardware. melonDS is usable but less exact than mGBA. |
| **Checking work** | `make compare` proves every change, and mGBA replays check the equivalent C. | No matching build. The only checks are behaviour comparisons in melonDS, which can't take our scripted inputs the way our mGBA runner does. |
| **Head start** | The Minish Cap decomp, which shares its engine, gives names and structs. | Our own GBA decomp. Where the DSi code reads the shared GBA tables, it probably mirrors our functions, which helps with naming. |

What this means for the plan:

- **A full decomp of the DSi game isn't worth it.** Your four features are a small part of its code. The rest is mostly the GBA engine rewritten, which we already have in C.
- **Targeted study is the right scale:** Ghidra with melonDS, starting from the shared data and the strings. For each feature, read only that code and reimplement it in our C, in our own structures.
  - **AI partner:** the largest piece of new logic, and the one most worth reading closely.
  - **Status screen and resolution:** mostly a matter of watching what the game does, plus a few constants.
  - **New levels:** mainly a data-format problem, eased by the GBA data they share.
- **A recomp** would only make sense to run the AI as-is instead of reimplementing it. It would need an ARM decoder of our own, and we'd also have to emulate the DS hardware around that code, a big job just to run one subsystem.

## Claude

I've saved the order to memory: 1, the new levels; 2, the resolution change; 3, the AI. The status screen isn't on the list yet.

Here's what the levels work would involve:

- **Our side first.** To load new levels, the PS2 port has to understand Four Swords' own level format: room headers, tilemaps, tilesets, entity lists and warps. A lot of that loading code is still in the mechanically translated part. So step one is hand-decompiling the Four Swords room and map loaders and naming those tables. That's useful for the port anyway.
- **Find the new data.** Some of the DSi map and graphics files are copied GBA data, and those parts line up with tables we already know. The bytes that have no GBA counterpart are the candidates for the new levels.
- **Work out the formats.** If the new levels use the same format as the GBA levels, little code is needed. If they were converted for the DSi engine, we'd read those loaders in Ghidra and write a converter that turns them into the GBA layout at build time.
- **Supply the files at runtime.** Like the ROM, DSi assets can't be committed. The port would read them from the user's own DSi ROM, the same way it uses their GBA ROM.

New levels also bring new text, and some may use new enemies or behaviour. Those would come out of the DSi code itself, so the levels work could pull in some Ghidra study earlier than planned.

The first concrete step is mapping our Four Swords room loaders and the files they read. I'd start there next, unless you want to keep going with the general decomp instead.

## User

What kind of work do you anticipate for this step?

## Claude

I'd expect about one focused session to map our side and a second for the DSi comparison. That depends on how much of the Four Swords loading path is still mechanically translated. I haven't checked yet, and that's the main unknown. Most of the work is reading and naming, not writing new code.

1. **Find the load path.** Trace from "the game changes rooms" to the code that copies the room's data into memory. The quickest route is an mGBA replay from our recordings that walks through a door. We log which functions run and which ROM tables they read, and the tile, palette and map uploads point at the loaders.
2. **Decompile those functions by hand.** I'd expect a few dozen: the room-transition logic, the loaders for tilesets, tilemaps, collision, palettes and entity lists, and the decompressors. The decompressors are probably the BIOS ones or near copies, as in Minish Cap. Minish Cap's decomp shares this engine, so its matching C and struct names should cover a good share of them. Everything gets the usual `make compare` or NONMATCHING checks.
3. **Name and type the data.** Turn the `gUnknown_08xxxxxx` tables these functions read into named, typed structs, such as a room header with its size, tileset ID, entity-list pointer and exits. This is where the level format becomes documented in code, which is what the DSi comparison needs.
4. **Write a small dump tool.** A host-side script that lists every Four Swords room from the user's ROM: its sizes, assets and entities, plus a rendered PNG of the room. It's a check that the format is right, since rendered rooms should look like the game, and it's the tool we'd later point at the DSi files.
5. **Docs and commits.** Walkthrough and planning doc entries, plus format notes the DSi work will refer back to.

Risks:

- **Indirect loading.** Function-pointer tables and per-level script data could make the trail harder to follow than a straight call chain.
- **Compression and packing.** Four Swords may pack its maps differently from Minish Cap, so not all of the Minish Cap code will carry over.
- **Overlap with A Link to the Past.** Some loaders may be shared with the A Link to the Past side of the cartridge, which widens the trace a little.

What this produces: a documented Four Swords level format in C and named data, and a tool that dumps and renders rooms. Once those exist, the DSi part becomes "run the same dump on the DSi files and see what differs" rather than open-ended reverse engineering.

## Claude

I've worked out how Four Swords stores its levels and written a tool that lists and renders them: [tools/fs_rooms.py](tools/fs_rooms.py). Run with `--png DIR`, it draws every stage map, and all 146 render correctly. The sub-rooms each stage is assembled from aren't drawn yet; that's the next piece. It's committed together with walkthrough Step 23 and the conversation archive; `make compare` still reports OK.

The format turned out to be almost the same as Minish Cap's:

- **Loader:** `sub_0801484C` is Minish Cap's map-data loader. It reads 12-byte records that each say where in the map data to read, where to load it, how big it is and whether it's compressed, or, for a destination of 0, which palette group to load.
- **Map data:** one shared block of map data starting at 0x0854F7E8. That's where the DSi `zelmap.bin` starts matching the GBA ROM, so the DSi game very likely kept the same data.
- **Stages:** 146 stages in 6 pools. Each stage has a fixed map of up to 63×63 metatiles in two layers, one of 6 tilesets, slots for random sub-rooms, four player start points, and a pointer to its enemies and objects.
- **Sub-rooms:** 216 in 4 pools. Each time a stage loads, the game picks one at random for each slot and stamps it into the map. Their own sizes and maps are decoded.
- **Tilesets:** tiles into VRAM, plus per-layer tables that say which tiles make up each metatile and what type each metatile is, plus a palette group.

Most of the code involved was already NONMATCHING C from earlier work, so this step was mainly working out what the data means. I haven't hand-decompiled any more of it yet.

One part is still unknown: which sub-room pool fills which stage pool. There are 6 stage pools but only 4 sub-room pools. My first renders filled every slot from the first sub-room pool and drew the wrong rooms, so the slots are left empty for now. Tracing the value both pickers index by in a replay should settle it.

Next, I'd work out that pool mapping so sub-rooms render too, then run the same decoding on the DSi map files. The parts that turn out not to match GBA data should be the new levels.

The renders are in `/tmp/claude-1000/-home-alex-Documents-zeldaalttp-ps2/93b91fe6-ec1b-4c3a-976d-9c1099efa5e9/scratchpad/rooms/`. I found the DSi tileset table, but I can't decode the tileset contents yet. Comparing bytes has run out, so the next step is reading the DSi game's loader code.

**Found:**
- **Tileset table:** at 0x020D70F0 in the DSi main program, one pointer per tileset (0–14). Tilesets 3 and 5 share a list, just as on the GBA, which confirms the numbering. An animation table for the 15 tilesets follows straight after it.
- **Records:** each tileset's list is the GBA format reworked. A record is {entry A + "more follows" bit, destination, entry B}; a destination of 0 means a palette group. The entry numbers point into `zelmap.bin` instead of a ROM offset. The destinations are DS background VRAM and four RAM buffers.
- **Stage maps:** stage *m* is `zelmap.bin` entries 64+2*m and 65+2*m.

**Not found: what the A and B entries hold.** So far B is always A+1. Their data doesn't line up with the GBA tileset parts: the GBA tilesets were compared against the DSi entries and agree by at most 30%. Some entries are just counting tables (0, 1, 2, …), and some are 0x8000 bytes, bigger than any GBA metatile table. So the DSi game converts the tiles and metatiles into its own layout. Guessing further from the bytes would waste time.

**Next step: read the DSi loader code.** The function that walks these tileset records will say what A and B hold and how metatiles become tiles. It's a single function, quick to find in Ghidra (free, on GitHub) by searching for references to 0x020D70F0. Once it's read, `dsi_zelmap.py` can render the new stages with their real graphics.

## Claude

To answer both properly I need to check where the DSi edits to existing GBA stages actually are.

- tool `Read`: /tmp/claude-1000/-home-alex-Documents-zeldaalttp-ps2/93b91fe6-ec1b-4c3a-976d-9c1099efa5e9/scratchpad/diff1.png

- tool `Read`: /tmp/claude-1000/-home-alex-Documents-zeldaalttp-ps2/93b91fe6-ec1b-4c3a-976d-9c1099efa5e9/scratchpad/diff58.png

## Claude

1. **No, but nearly.** The DSi game reuses most GBA maps unchanged, with small edits to some.
2. **No, not past the map's own edges.** But 320×240 would show more of what lies just outside each play area: the filler around it, and sometimes separate parts of the same map that the GBA screen never showed at once.

**1. Same maps?**

I compared every GBA stage map the game uses with its DSi counterpart, metatile by metatile:
- Of the 111 stage maps the stages use, 71 are identical and 40 differ.
- The differences are small design tweaks, not changes for the bigger screen. Stage map 1 has a reshaped water channel; stage map 58 has a rearranged lake shoreline.
- Most edits are in the middle of the maps, not at the borders. One outlier, stage map 94, has over 2,000 changed metatiles and is effectively reworked. I haven't looked at it yet.
- Sub-rooms are similar: 379 layers are identical and 55 are small edits.
- The 18 Anniversary stages are new.
- The map size didn't change: every stage is still 63×63 metatiles (1008×1008 px).

So the DSi's 256×192 screen needed no map changes. The DSi code centres the camera on 128/96 instead of 120/80 and clamps it to the same 1008-pixel map size.

**2. Would 320×240 show outside the map?**

- **Past the map edges: no.** The camera is clamped to the map size, as on the GBA and the DSi. At 320×240 it simply stops 320 px from the right edge and 240 px from the bottom.
- **Past the playable areas inside a map: yes, more of it.** Each 1008×1008 map is a canvas holding one or more play areas surrounded by filler (rock, brick or sky patterns), and sometimes separate areas side by side. Compared with the GBA, 320×240 shows an extra 40 px on every side; the DSi shows only an extra 8 px left and right and 16 px top and bottom. The filler is drawn tiles, so it won't look broken. Near the edge of an area, though, players could see neighbouring rooms or hidden bonus areas that the GBA screen kept off-view. That's a design side effect rather than a rendering bug, and the DSi already accepts a milder version of it.

Two bigger issues come with the wider view, and neither is about the maps:
- **The map buffer is too small.** The GBA game streams the map into a 256×256 hardware tilemap that wraps around. A 320-pixel-wide view doesn't fit in it. The PS2 renderer has to draw from the full 64×64-metatile map in RAM instead of copying the GBA's background buffer. That's straightforward, since the full map sits in the layer buffers we've already decoded.
- **Enemies and objects at the screen edges.** The game probably decides which objects to update and draw based on the 240×160 screen. If so, with a wider view, players would see enemies frozen or appearing late near the edges. The DSi must have widened those ranges too, so its code can show where.

I haven't checked how the camera behaves in boss rooms, transitions, or any mode that sets a smaller camera area than the full map. Those are the places where a wider view is most likely to show something unintended.

## User

How much of the PS2 port will rely on decomp code, and how much on decomp?

## Claude

Your question names "decomp" twice, so I've read it as asking how much of the port will be the game's decompiled code and how much will be new code written for the PS2. If you meant hand-decompiled C against mechanically translated C, that's the earlier table: about 20% hand-written and 80% mechanical by code size.

These estimates are by code size. The PS2 and DSi parts are projections, since that work hasn't started yet.

**Code from the GBA ROM: the large majority**

Everything the game itself does comes from the decomp: game logic, enemies and objects, the room and stage loading we just mapped, and items, text and menus. That's about 1.2 MB of original GBA code. Today 20% of it is hand-written C and 80% is mechanically translated, and it all runs in the replay checks. Over time the parts the port touches most get hand-written. The rest can stay mechanical, since it already behaves the same.

**New PS2 code: a thin layer, probably a few tens of KB**

| Piece | What it replaces |
|---|---|
| Rendering | The GBA graphics hardware: background tilemaps, sprites, palettes and blending, drawn with the PS2's Graphics Synthesizer (GS). This is the largest piece. |
| Split screen | Four game states, or one shared state with four camera views (the design choice still to make), in place of linked GBAs. |
| Audio | The GBA sound driver's output, through the PS2's sound processor. The sound driver itself is decompiled C, and a C version also exists in other pret projects. |
| Input, saves, startup | Controllers instead of the GBA pad, memory card instead of EEPROM, PS2 startup instead of the GBA boot ROM. |
| Link cable | Replaced by direct data passing between players, instead of emulating the serial port. |

**From the DSi version: new code modelled on it, no DSi code copied**

- **New levels:** mostly data. The 18 stages use the GBA formats, so the decompiled loaders take them with a small adapter. Any new enemy or object behaviour gets written in C from reading the DSi code.
- **Wider view:** a few camera and range constants in decomp code, plus the renderer drawing from the full map.
- **AI partner:** new code, the largest of the three, written from studying the DSi game.

Overall, by code size, more than 90% of the port will be decompiled GBA code. The PS2 layer and the DSi-inspired features make up the rest. The new code is small, but the risk is concentrated there: the renderer, the split-screen design and the AI partner.
