## Claude

Yes. Nothing I've found blocks it, and our existing C, both the translated and the hand-written, can be used as it is. But it's several sessions of work, not one. Here's where things stand and what it would take.

**Compiling for the PS2 is close.** I built all of our C with the PS2 compiler (EE GCC with ps2sdk, both already installed). Once old-style C is allowed (`-std=gnu99`, plus a few warnings that newer GCC treats as errors), about 20 real C errors are left:
- some casts used as lvalues;
- a few conflicting function prototypes;
- one duplicate `static`;
- one struct-size check.

All quick fixes. The other failures are assembly: `asm(".include")` lines for functions that aren't C yet, and Thumb entry stubs in the generated global-state files. The PS2 build drops both. The C translations of those functions already exist in `src/auto/`; the stubs need a few C replacements.

**Memory addresses can stay as they are.** The game's C and the ROM's data tables are full of absolute GBA addresses (RAM at 0x02000000 and 0x03000000, ROM at 0x08000000). ps2sdk's `PutTLBEntry` can map those virtual addresses onto PS2 RAM. Every pointer then works unchanged, and the ROM data is read from the user's own `baserom.gba` at run time, so nothing gets committed. Hardware registers (0x04000000) and video memory get mapped to RAM the same way, and the PS2 side reads them each frame.

**New PS2 code a first boot needs:**

| Piece | Work |
|---|---|
| Startup | Map the memory, load the ROM, run the game's main loop. |
| BIOS calls | About 15 C functions: memory copy and fill, decompression, division, square root. |
| Interrupts | At each PS2 vsync, run the game's vblank handler and set the display status bits it polls. |
| Rendering | A software version of the GBA graphics chip (background modes 0–2, sprites, palettes, basic blending) drawing 240×160 into a texture shown through the Graphics Synthesizer. This is the largest piece. |
| Input | The PS2 pad written into the GBA's key register. |
| Sound, saves | Muted and stubbed at first. |

**Milestones:**
1. Everything compiles and links into a PS2 ELF.
2. It boots in PCSX2 (software renderer) without crashing, following the TLB-miss rules from CLAUDE.md.
3. The title screen appears through the software graphics chip.
4. One player can play Four Swords.
5. Split-screen multiplayer, then sound, saves and the DSi features.

**Risks:**
- **Machine-level assumptions in the C.** Struct layout, unaligned reads (the GBA rotates them, the PS2 faults), and integer edge cases may differ between ARM and MIPS. The replay checks against mGBA, frame by frame, will catch these.
- **The Four Swords game mode.** It expects linked GBAs, so getting past the multiplayer setup screens is likely to need the link-cable replacement earlier than planned.

If you want to go ahead, I'll start on milestone 1: a PS2 build target, the C fixes, the stub replacements, and a link with the memory mapping.

## User

As far as rendering, what code can we reuse from mGBA?

- tool `Bash`: Inspect mGBA software renderer files, deps, license

## Claude

Most of mGBA's software renderer can be reused, about 2,300 lines of plain C. Its license allows that, with one condition on the files we take.

**What we can take**

| File (in `reference/mgba`) | Lines | Does |
|---|---|---|
| `src/gba/renderers/video-software.c` | 1,059 | Frame and scanline driver, register handling, windows, blending and brightness |
| `src/gba/renderers/software-mode0.c` | 588 | Tile backgrounds (the mode Four Swords uses) |
| `src/gba/renderers/software-obj.c` | 421 | Sprites, including scaled and rotated ones |
| `src/gba/renderers/software-bg.c` | 228 | Scaled and rotated, and bitmap, backgrounds (modes 1–5) |
| `software-private.h`, `video-software.h`, `common.c` | ~220 | Shared helpers and the renderer struct |

It's independent of mGBA's CPU emulation. It sits behind a small interface: we tell it about writes to video memory, palette, sprite data and video registers, ask it to draw each scanline, then collect the 240×160 frame. Its other dependencies are a few mGBA utility headers (memory, colour types, register names), which are easy to trim or stub.

`gl.c` (mGBA's OpenGL renderer) isn't reusable on the PS2. It's still a useful model if we later render natively on the Graphics Synthesizer instead of in software.

**License: MPL 2.0 (file-level copyleft)**
- We can include those files in the port without changing the license of the rest of the project.
- They keep their MPL notices.
- Any changes we make to those files must be published under MPL as well, which happens anyway with the repo on GitHub.
- No noncommercial restriction, unlike FourSwordsRecomp's PolyForm license.

**How it fits our plan**
- **Feeding it:** the game writes video memory and registers directly into the mapped GBA memory. Each frame, the PS2 side hands the renderer that memory and the register values, then draws the 160 lines.
- **Mid-frame effects:** the game changes some registers partway through a frame, through its scanline table driven by direct memory transfers during horizontal blanking. Drawing line by line with those per-line values reproduces them, as mGBA does.
- **Speed:** mGBA renders at full speed on much weaker machines while also emulating the CPU, so rendering one GBA screen on the EE is cheap. Four split-screen views means four renderer instances, which should still fit, but I'd measure it in PCSX2 early.

**Where we'd change it**
- **Wider resolution:** the renderer assumes a 240-pixel-wide screen, and its background wrap-around depends on the GBA's tilemap sizes. A 320×240 view needs those widened. That's a modification to MPL files, so those changes are published under MPL too.
- **Output:** frames go to a Graphics Synthesizer texture via gsKit instead of mGBA's frontend.

So the plan's biggest piece, the graphics-chip replacement, becomes mostly integration work instead of a from-scratch renderer.

## Claude

Yes, it ran out of memory, and the process the kernel killed was my build.

- **The kill:** at `[924385]` the kernel killed `agbcc`, PID 853080. It had grown to about 5.4 GB of RAM. That's the same PID I saw earlier with 10 minutes of CPU time, compiling the huge generated global-state file. It ran inside the IDE's process group (`app-org.chromium.Chromium-770498.scope`), which is why the IDE went down with it.
- **The earlier entry** at `[704378]` is a separate, older kill of a `python3` process at about 5.9 GB, roughly 2.5 days earlier by the timestamps. It may have been one of my analysis scripts from an earlier session. I haven't confirmed which.

What caused it: my `gstate2c.py` fix made each global-state copy run up to the next real function instead of stopping at the first label inside it. For `rom1`, whose functions are all pinned in large groups, that produces a few enormous C functions. agbcc, GCC 2.95, at `-O2` on functions that size uses memory without bound.

Fixes before I run that build again:
1. **Compile generated global-state files at a lower optimization level.** For the ARM `AUTO_C` build that's agbcc `-O1` or `-O0`; the PS2 build already uses `-O1`. Speed isn't critical there; those files are a bridge until the code is hand-written.
2. **Cap each compile's memory** with `ulimit -v`, about 3 GB, so a runaway compiler fails with an error instead of triggering the OOM killer.
3. **Build with `-j2` instead of `-j8`** for these steps.
4. **Run long builds outside the IDE's process group** (for example with `systemd-run --user --scope`), so even a kill can't take the IDE down.

The uncommitted work since the last commit is still on disk. That includes the PS2 linker script, `bios.c`, `tlb.c` and the `gstate2c.py` changes; nothing was lost. Should I apply these safeguards and carry on with the PS2 link?

## Claude

The PS2 build now boots in PCSX2 and runs the game's main loop: more than 1,200 frames with no crash, TLB miss or stall. Nothing is drawn yet, so the only proof it's running is the frame counter and trace output over the serial console. It's committed, with walkthrough Step 24, and `make compare` still reports OK.

**Memory safeguards.** You confirmed the OOM kill came from my agbcc build at about 5.4 GB. Generated files now compile at `-O0` with a memory cap, and long builds run in a 6 GB systemd scope. That scope later contained an `asm2c` blow-up without touching the IDE.

**What it took to boot, beyond compiling and linking:**
- **Memory mapping.** PCSX2's kernel refuses `PutTLBEntry`, so the GBA regions go into its unused TLB entries instead.
- **ARM routines.** The game runs four ARM routines from IWRAM, including the entity update loop; they're now in C. Indirect calls to GBA addresses go through a resolver.
- **Two bugs in my translators,** found here but present on the ARM side too:
  - Code after a label inside a function was never translated. The ARM build hid it by running that code natively.
  - Some functions read data stored inside the neighbouring function, which only worked because the code sat side by side.
- **Hardware side effects.** DMA, interrupt flags, the scanline counter and the save chip each blocked boot until emulated. My first plan, trapping writes to the I/O page, doesn't work in PCSX2, which never raises the exception. The translated code now calls an I/O layer for those registers instead.
- **Watchdog.** A once-a-second report names the last function entered, which is how each hang was found.

**Not done:**
- No rendering, so nothing appears on screen yet.
- No vsync pacing (it runs at about 100 frames per second), no controller input, no sound.
- Saves aren't implemented: the save chip always reports ready and reads back as empty.
- The ARM-side replay check hasn't been rerun since the translator fixes; that's worth doing before relying on them.

Next is rendering: integrating mGBA's software renderer to draw the GBA screen through the Graphics Synthesizer, plus vsync pacing. That will show whether the game is really reaching the title screen.

## Claude

The PS2 port now draws the game and reaches the file select screen in PCSX2, with controller input wired up. The Nintendo/Capcom logo and the title screen match mGBA's frames, and it ran over 22,000 frames (60+ seconds) without a crash. Headless test runs can't press buttons, so I haven't confirmed that the controller actually drives the game.

**To try it:** load `build/ps2/zeldaalttp.elf` in PCSX2 (System → Boot ELF) with a controller on port 1. Circle = A, Cross = B, L1/R1 = L/R, Start and Select as themselves, D-pad or left stick to move.

**Rendering:** mGBA's software renderer is now in the repo under `src/ps2/mgba` (MPL-2.0, with its license and source version noted). `src/ps2/video.c` hands it the screen state each frame, shows the result through the Graphics Synthesizer and waits for vsync, so the game runs at 60 Hz. A few frames are also saved as image files next to the ELF, so I can compare them with mGBA without a window.

**Bugs fixed along the way:**
- **Reset every frame.** The keypad register read as "every button held", which includes the soft-reset combination, so the game reset continuously.
- **Endless loop on MIPS.** A `void` function was called through a table that expects an `int` result. On ARM the result happened to be 0; on MIPS it was leftover data, so the loop never ended. It now returns 0, and the matching build is unchanged.
- **Hard hang leaving the title.** The PS2 compiler leaves gaps between objects' lookup tables, so lookups for the translated code failed. The failed lookup then jumped into data as if it were code and froze the processor. Table entries are now padded so there are no gaps.

## Claude

Right now only one renderer fits, and only just. Yes, it's CPU-driven: mGBA's renderer runs entirely on the EE and the Graphics Synthesizer only displays the finished texture.

I measured it with the EE's cycle counter in PCSX2. At 294.9 MHz, a 60 Hz frame gives the EE 4.9 million cycles:

| Per frame | Cycles | Share of a frame |
|---|---|---|
| Rendering the file select | about 4.0–4.1 million | about 82% |
| Game logic (everything else) | about 94,000 | about 2% |

The game logic is cheap; rendering is nearly the whole cost. That's about 100 cycles per pixel, so four views (36 million cycles a frame) are out of reach this way. PCSX2 counts EE cycles approximately and largely ignores cache misses, so on real hardware it's probably worse.

There are two ways to get to four views:

1. **Optimize the software renderer:** perhaps 2–3× faster.
   - **Don't redraw unchanged scanlines.** At the moment I mark everything dirty every frame.
   - **Use 16-bit output** (mGBA's `COLOR_16_BIT` build option).
   - **Compiler flags:** `-O3` and EE-specific options.
   - **Cheaper input each frame:** feed only the registers and palette entries that changed, instead of everything.

   That might reach one view comfortably and two at a squeeze, still not four.
2. **Draw with the Graphics Synthesizer:** the approach mGBA's OpenGL renderer takes.
   - **What changes:** the EE converts VRAM into GS textures only when it changes. Each frame it then just sends draw lists: one textured strip per background layer and one quad per sprite, in priority order.
   - **Cost:** the GS has fill rate to spare (four 240×160 screens is trivial for it), so the EE's cost drops to building small display lists, a few hundred thousand cycles per view.
   - **What's harder:** priorities, windows and blending have to be mapped onto GS blending modes. Some GBA effects, such as colour effects across layers and mid-frame changes from scanline effects, need care, for example drawing per scanline band where the game changes registers mid-frame.

For split-screen with four players, option 2 is the path that scales. I'd keep the software renderer as the reference: render the same frame both ways and compare, the same way we compare against mGBA now.

There's also a design question that affects this. If the port runs one shared game for all four players rather than four separate GBAs, the backgrounds are the same map seen from four cameras. Once tiles are GS textures, they can be uploaded once and drawn four times, which makes option 2 cheaper still.

The cost measurement is committed: it logs every 10 seconds, so later changes can be compared against it.

## User

What do we need to make the replay work on the PS2 build?

## Claude

The main gap is that session 1 is a two-GBA Four Swords session. The PS2 build runs one GBA, and Four Swords won't start a game without at least two linked players. So replaying it needs the link-cable replacement anyway, which the port needs for multiplayer regardless.

1. **Two game instances in one PS2 program.** All of the game's state lives at fixed GBA addresses (RAM, I/O, VRAM), so two copies can't share them as they are. But we map those addresses with TLB entries already, so switching instance just means repointing the entries (7 of them) at the other GBA's memory blocks. The PS2-side state also has to be per instance: the renderer, DMA and EEPROM, the global-state CPU registers, and the trace ring. Each instance runs a frame in turn. That's moderate work, and it's also the structure the split-screen port needs.
2. **Link cable.**
   - **Serial registers:** emulate multiplayer serial transfers between the instances, with the serial interrupt the game waits on. In link mode the main loop paces itself with `IntrWait(SERIAL)` rather than vblank.
   - **ARM handler:** the game's serial interrupt handler is ARM code it copies to RAM (`0x08000318`), so it needs a C port like the other ARM routines.
   - **Timing:** this is the delicate part. mGBA runs the GBAs in lockstep with cycle-level timing. We'd exchange data at the same points in the frame, which should be enough because the game's protocol is frame-synchronous, but I'd expect some debugging.
3. **A recording from power-on.** Session 1 starts from mGBA savestates (`state0.ss`) taken mid-game. Those hold CPU registers and stacks that mean nothing to the C port. `tools/fs_walk.inputs` (3,921 frames from power-on, two GBAs, `start_linked` saves) is replayable as it is, and new longer recordings can start from boot too.
4. **Scripted input.** Read the per-frame inputs from a file instead of the controller (a small change in `input.c`). Inputs are keyed by vblank count, so frames need to stay aligned: one `VBlankIntrWait` is one vblank on our side, and any lag frames on the GBA would shift it. Comparing state catches that.
5. **Comparing against mGBA.**
   - **On the PS2 side:** dump RAM (and screenshots, which already work) at chosen frames.
   - **On the mGBA side:** dump at the same frames with `mgba_run --dump`.
   - **The check:** diff the two. This is the accuracy check CLAUDE.md calls for, and it shows the first frame where the port diverges.
6. **Hardware the game logic may notice.** Timers, if the game reads them (random numbers or timing), and the remaining I/O registers. Sound and per-scanline effects only affect output, not game state, so they can wait.

**Order I'd suggest:** 1, then 2 with `fs_walk` as the test (4 is small, so it comes along), then 5 to find divergences, then longer recordings. Step 1 is also the base for split-screen, and step 2 for any Four Swords gameplay at all, so none of this is throwaway work.

## User

Let's start with two game instances. However, we can cheat a bit and not emulate the link cable. All we really need is for game data to be shared between players, like a regular split screen game. How does this change the plan?

## Claude

It simplifies the link part a lot, but it doesn't remove the need for separate game instances. Here's why, and what changes.

**How Four Swords shares a game.** Each GBA runs the whole game world itself, as the player whose ID it has: its camera, its HUD, its Link as "the local player". The link cable doesn't carry a shared world. Each frame, every GBA sends a small packet (its inputs and some sync data) and receives everyone else's. Because all four simulations are deterministic and get the same inputs, they stay identical.

So the game code has no notion of "one world, several views". A genuinely single shared world with four cameras would mean restructuring how the decompiled code treats the local player: camera, HUD, rendering, menus. That's possible later, since we have the source, but it's a big project.

**The shortcut that works now.** Keep one instance per player and cheat at the packet level instead of emulating the link cable:

| Before (emulate the cable) | Now (cheat at the packet layer) |
|---|---|
| Serial registers, transfer timing, serial interrupts | At each frame boundary, take each instance's outgoing packet and drop it straight into the others' receive buffers |
| Port the ARM serial interrupt handler | Not needed |
| Match mGBA's lockstep timing | Exchanges are frame-synchronous and deterministic by construction |
| Main loop waits on `IntrWait(SERIAL)` | Treat it as the frame wait |

The registers the game reads at startup to detect a link and its own player number get fixed values per instance. Instances are cheap: game logic measured about 94,000 cycles a frame, so four is roughly 8% of the EE. Rendering is the real cost, which we discussed. Each instance renders its own player's view, which is exactly the split screen.

**Revised plan:**
1. **Instances:** two game instances, switched by repointing the TLB entries at each instance's memory blocks, plus per-instance PS2-side state (renderer, DMA, EEPROM, global-state registers). Unchanged from before.
2. **Packet exchange:** find the game's link layer: where it builds the outgoing packet, where it reads received packets, and the flags marking a transfer as done. Then write `ps2_link_exchange()` to run between frames. This replaces cable emulation. Understanding the game's link code takes some reverse-engineering, but far less than timing-accurate serial emulation.
3. **Replay:** inputs from a file per instance, so `fs_walk` can run on the PS2.
4. **Comparing with mGBA:** RAM dumps at matching frames. Exact agreement with mGBA isn't guaranteed any more, since mGBA delivers packets with real cable timing. If the protocol is frame-locked as I expect, state should still match, and the comparison will show whether it does.

There's one more option, for the shared data that isn't gameplay state (ROM, decompressed tiles, maps). It already exists only once, because every instance maps the same ROM, and later the GS textures can be shared too.

I'll start on step 1, two instances with TLB switching, unless you want to change the plan first.

- **Per-instance PS2 state:** renderer, textures, EEPROM data and save file, and the controller port.

2. **Key Technical Concepts:**
   - **FS level format:**
     - Stage descriptors live in pools gUnknown_0842B8A8[6] (146 stages): [0] map, [1] tileset, [2] slots, [4+2i] slot positions, [12..19] player starts, +20 object layers.
     - Sub-room pools gUnknown_0842B8CC[4] (216 entries); room pool = stage pool.
     - Map data: MapDataDefinition records loaded by sub_0801484C, relative to gUnknown_0854F7E8.
     - Tilesets: gUnknown_08146078; stage maps: gUnknown_08146090; room maps: gUnknown_0814627C; room sizes: gUnknown_081465E0; palettes: gUnknown_08429750 (base 0x0844DD74).
   - **DSi (FSAE):**
     - zelmap.bin = NDS file 24 (index of offset/size pairs; record words A/B = the two halves of one pair, entry = A/2; LZ11).
     - zeldat.bin = file 20 (palettes).
     - ARM9 tables: tilesets 0x020D70F0, stage maps 0x020D7660, palette groups 0x021039B8, new-stage pool 0x02103DD4.
     - 18 new stages, map indices 123–140, using tilesets 6–14.
     - Camera centres on 128/96.
   - **PS2 port architecture:**
     - `NONMATCHING=1 AUTO_C=1` ARM build generates src/auto/*.c and *_gstate.c / *_gstate_ps2.c.
     - The PS2 build is Makefile.ps2 (EE gcc -std=gnu99).
     - tools/ps2/struct_align.py: every non-packed struct/union gets aligned(4) (agbcc rule); it also strips ARM asm and rewrites cast-as-lvalue.
   - **TLB mapping:** PutTLBEntry is refused by the kernel, so free entries 39–47 are written with `_SetTLBEntry`.
   - **ICALL resolver:** handles indirect calls.
   - **I/O:** io.c handles I/O side effects through the R*/W* macros (PCSX2 doesn't raise TLB-modified, so the store-trap approach failed). It emulates DMA, the EEPROM, and VCOUNT advancing per read.
   - **Rendering:** mGBA software renderer, vendored (MPL-2.0); costs about 4.0M of the 4.9M EE cycles per frame.
   - **Instances:**
     - Two game instances run in threads with cooperative scheduling at VBlankIntrWait.
     - The TLB is remapped per instance; each instance gets 1 MB physical at 0x01800000 + i·1 MB.

4. **Errors and fixes:**
   - **OOM (user confirmed via dmesg).** agbcc was killed at 5.4 GB on a 147 MB rom1_gstate.c. That file came from treating grouped copy names as inner labels; fixed. Safeguards were added (systemd scope, ulimit, -j1).
   - **Copy blobs.** Separate per-copy blobs broke reads of neighbouring literal pools; now one contiguous blob per object.
   - **No TLB-modified exception in PCSX2,** so stores to I/O weren't trapped; switched to the macro-based io.c.
   - **Early hangs** (fixed in turn):
     - m4a VCOUNT wait;
     - DMA3 wait;
     - EEPROM polling (the 0x0D000000 page);
     - KEYINPUT=0 meant the reset combo was held every frame;
     - the void/int table loop (sub_0800D87C).
   - **Misaligned gstate tables:** 8-byte alignment with 12-byte entries left gaps; padded entries to 16 bytes.
   - **False stall:** pcsx2_run needs the `heartbeat: vblank N frame M` line format.
   - **Replay regression** (120 fails): bisected to gstate C at -O0; reverted to -O2, giving 1328 ok / 24 fail (baseline).
   - **Two instances, VCOUNT:** VCOUNT toggling in the ISR wasn't seen by the instance thread (root cause unclear); replaced with VCOUNT advancing per read.
   - **Compile errors fixed during editing:** 'o' undeclared ordering in io.c; ps2_trace_on undeclared in frame.c.

   - **Working so far:** the PS2 single instance reached the file select, ran for 60+ s, and saves worked (the mGBA save loads).
   - **Two instances:**
     - Instance 0 completes its first frame, and instance 1 starts.
     - Then instance 1 hits FATAL "gstate_run 00000000: sp 00000000 outside EWRAM (lr 00000000, instance 1)".
     - The instance-1 trace shows: AgbMain → initialize_gba → main_disable_interrupts → setup_interrupt_handler → auto sub_080679CC → auto sub_08135BCC → auto sub_08135C3C → auto sub_08134684 (m4aSoundInit) → gs sub_08134A84 → gs sub_08133E64 → gs sub_08133E7E → run 0.
     - The translated gs_sub_08133E7E pushes r0 at sp, then returns via `lr` (if even → GSTATE_STORE; gCpu.r[15]=lr; return). lr/sp/gCpu are evidently 0 in instance 1, i.e. the gCpu state is zero or invalid; the cause is not yet determined.
     - The per-instance EWRAM mapping was verified correct (tlb check log: c0de0000 / c0de0001 for instances 0 and 1).
     - Hypotheses still open:
       - gCpu was wiped or not set up: gstate_enter_c's sp default fires only when sp is outside 0x02038000–0x02040000;
       - something about thread context and the initial gCpu;
       - a difference between instance 0 and instance 1 initial state.

## Claude

Two game instances now run side by side in PCSX2. Each reaches the file select with its own controller port and save file. The matching build still reports `zeldaalttp.gba: OK`, and the work is committed as `c22cf4a`.

- **The crash:** the second instance died at once because of PCSX2 itself. Its EE recompiler fixes the memory location of a constant address when it compiles a block of code. So code first compiled while instance 0 was mapped kept reading and writing instance 0's memory after I switched the mapping to instance 1. A real PS2 wouldn't do this, but PCSX2 is the test bench.
- **The fix:** the GBA address space is now mapped once onto a single "live" block. Switching instances copies the running instance's memory out and the next one's in, about 387 KB each way. The main loop now runs, draws and saves each instance in turn, so there are two switches per frame ([tlb.c](src/ps2/tlb.c), [main.c](src/ps2/main.c)).
- **Speed:** the pair runs at 30 fps, not 60. Drawing two screens with mGBA's renderer takes about 8.4M of the 4.9M EE cycles available per frame. The two games plus the memory copies take about 2M more. Moving the drawing onto the Graphics Synthesizer would fix this, and it's needed for 4 players anyway.
- **Still to fix:** PCSX2 reports "TLB Miss" lines at the file select: a sprite routine (`gs_sub_08003870`) reads fields through a null pointer. It only happens with the save file the game wrote for player 2. A one-instance run with that save does it too, so it's an existing bug, not a two-instance one. I've noted it in the walkthrough as the next thing to fix.

After that, the agreed plan is sharing game data between the two players, then scripted input so the replay can be checked against mGBA.

## Claude

A scripted replay now runs in PCSX2, but not yet with the recorded inputs unchanged. Two linked game instances start from empty saves, go through Four Swords' link lobby and Choose a Stage, and enter the same stage together, each screen showing both Links. That's from the 2-player replay build; the default 4-player build has no input scripts and wasn't rerun. The final check ran 6,680 frames with no crashes or TLB misses; an earlier run went past 15,000. Committed as `2d15058`.

The intro replay (`tests/intro_linked.inputs`) needs extra presses: the PS2 reaches the lobby about 200 frames later than mGBA, so the recorded presses run out before it's ready. I added A/Start presses after frame 1,400 in the build folder's copy only, not in the test file. Those presses also pause the game once it's in the stage ("P1 PAUSE!"). Frame-by-frame comparison with mGBA doesn't line up yet for the same reason.

`fs_walk.inputs` isn't usable here: it walks into A Link to the Past, whose main loop never finishes a frame on the PS2.

What made it work:
- **Link between instances** ([link.c](src/ps2/link.c)): no serial timing or interrupts. After every frame, each instance's outgoing words are copied into the others' receive registers. Then a C port of the game's link-cable handler runs on each instance's memory. Each instance sees itself as connected, with player 1 as the host and its own player number.
- **Scripted input**: `host:replay_p<n>.inputs`, in the mGBA runner's format, replaces controller n.
- **Four Swords only**: the PS2 build now boots like `fs_only.gba`, so picking a file starts Four Swords. `INSTANCES=n` sets the player count.

Bugs fixed on the way:
- **Link helper**: the game calls a small routine it copied into RAM as ARM code, which on the PS2 ran GBA bytes as MIPS and froze the EE. It's now ported to C.
- **Game switch**: when the main loop returns, the instance thread now restarts it instead of exiting.
- **Code stored as data**: some hand-written routines in the disassembly were bytes rather than instructions, so they were never translated. Pointers to them couldn't be adjusted for the PS2. One function is now written as instructions (same ROM bytes). As a general fallback, a ROM address with no translated entry is mapped onto the translated copy of that function. The translator also no longer rejects functions that start with data tables, cutting untranslated functions from 24 to 18.
- **Division by zero**: the GBA returns 0, and the game relies on that. The PS2's trap handler now does the same. Crash reports also now go to the log; before, they were silently lost.

The matching build is still OK, and the GBA-side replay check is unchanged at 1,328 ok / 24 fail. The walkthrough has a Step 28 entry.

Next could be lining the replay up with mGBA frame by frame, so the original recording works unmodified and RAM can be compared. Or players 3–4 over the same link, or the 30 fps rendering cost.

2. **Key Technical Concepts:**
   - **Instance memory: copy-swap, not TLB remap.** PCSX2's EE recompiler bakes host pointers for constant addresses (recVTLB.cpp `vtlb_DynGenWrite_Const`), so repointing the TLB doesn't work there.
     - One fixed live block at phys 0x01800000.
     - Each instance's backing copy is at 0x01900000 + i MB (kseg0).
     - `ps2_tlb_select` copies the used regions out and in: EWRAM 0x40000, IWRAM 0x8000, IO/pal/OAM 0x400, VRAM 0x18000.
   - **Frame loop:** each instance in turn is selected, runs one frame (cooperative threads, woken at VBlankIntrWait), then is rendered, gets its input and saves. Then `ps2_link_exchange`, then present.
   - **Link layer** (src/rom2.c):
     - Struct at 0x02030790:
       - +0 parent(8)/child;
       - +1 state; +2 ever-received mask; +3 this-frame mask; +4 packet queued; +5 packet received;
       - +6 start request; +7 error; +8 connect counter; +9; +0xB frame counter;
       - +0x14 send idx; +0x18 recv idx; +0x1C/+0x20 queued/sending packet; +0x24/+0x28/+0x2C receive buffers (4×28 bytes).
     - A packet is 13 transfers: 0xFEFE, then 12 halfwords per player.
     - `sub_080368D8` resets the link if `unk2 != unk3`.
     - Lobby handler: `sub_080369B4`, state in `gUnknown_03000FC0`.
   - **SIOCNT read override:** SD=1, SI = (inst ? 1 : 0), ID = inst.
   - **Raw GBA ROM addresses** kept as bytes in the asm: the mapping table `ps2_gba_copies` comes from tools/ps2/gba_copies.py (630 copies).
   - **gstate2c:** functions starting with data are now allowed (24 native-only functions down to 18).
   - **GBA division by zero returns 0** (libgcc `Ldiv0`); the PS2 trap handler emulates it.
   - **FS_ONLY on PS2** (default on); `INSTANCES` is a Makefile option.
   - **Scripted input:** files `host:replay_p<n>.inputs`.
   - **PCSX2 window capture:** run with `env -u WAYLAND_DISPLAY DISPLAY=:77 GDK_BACKEND=x11 XDG_SESSION_TYPE=x11 QT_QPA_PLATFORM=xcb` on an Xvfb :77, then capture with `xwd -root | ffmpeg`.

3. **Files and Code Sections:**
   - **src/ps2/tlb.c**
     - Copy-swap design, `SAVED(i)`, `ps2_cur_instance = -1` initially.
     - `sRegions` with `used` sizes.
     - `ps2_tlb_map` maps the live block and zeroes each saved copy (KEYINPUT 0x3FF at SAVED + 0x48130).
     - New `void *ps2_inst_ptr(int inst, u32 a)`: the live address for the current instance, else the saved copy.
   - **src/ps2/main.c**
     - `#ifndef INSTANCES / #define INSTANCES 4`; `int ps2_instances = INSTANCES;`.
     - `instance_main` loops `for(;;) AgbMain();` (crt0 re-inits on game switch).
     - Loop per instance: select, Start/Wakeup, SleepThread, render, input, save. Then `ps2_link_exchange(); ps2_video_present(INSTANCES)`.
   - **src/ps2/video.c**
     - 2x2 layout for 3–4 players.
     - Static `sPixels[MAX_INSTANCES][TEX_W*GBA_H]` (memalign returned NULL with 4 instances).
     - Game-cost accounting via sFrameRender.
     - Dump frames currently at `n == 1300 || 1600 || 2000 || 2400 || 2800`.
   - **src/ps2/link.c** (new)
     - `handler(i, m)`: C port of sub_0800C7E8 on instance memory.
     - `ps2_link_take()`: port of the EWRAM ARM helper from 0x08000318. Swaps +0x28/+0x2C, returns +5 and clears it.
     - `ps2_link_exchange()`: while the parent's SIOCNT has 0x80 set (max 16), gather SIOMLT_SEND (0xFFFF for absent players) and run the handler on all instances.
     - `ps2_link_siocnt(inst, v)`.
   - **src/ps2/io.c:** SIOCNT read (offsets 0x128/0x129, sizes 1/2/4) goes through `ps2_link_siocnt`.
   - **src/rom2.c:** in `sub_0800C6A8`, `#ifdef PLATFORM_PS2 u8 ok = ps2_link_take(); #else` the original cast call.

The video modes are in, and two players now show one above the other in 4:3 480p, P1 on top and P2 below, each centred. That's the screenshot I sent; both screens play the stage in PCSX2 with no TLB misses. I tested 240p, 480p 16:9 and 720p with one player in PCSX2. I didn't run 480i or plain 480p with one player, though 480p is the same mode the two-player run uses.

**Modes** ([video.c](src/ps2/video.c)):

| Mode | Single player | Tested in PCSX2 |
|---|---|---|
| 240p (single-player default) | 1:1, centred in 320×240 | yes |
| 480i | 480×320, centred in 640×480 | no |
| 480p | 480×320, centred in 640×480 | no (two-player run uses it) |
| 480p 16:9 | 720×480 inside the 854×480 anamorphic frame | yes |
| 720p | 960×640, centred in 1280×720 | yes |

- **Your spec didn't cover two sizes:** 480i single player and 720p single player. I picked 2× for 480i and 4× for 720p.
- **Two-player size:** each screen is 360×240 (1.5×), the largest that fits a half.
- **Filtering:** sizes that aren't a whole multiple (1.5×, and the 16:9 frame squeezed into a 640-wide buffer) use smoothing, so pixels don't come out uneven. Whole multiples stay sharp.
- **How the mode is chosen:** until there's a menu, it's set at build time with `make -f Makefile.ps2 VIDEO_MODE=0..4`. Without it, the build uses 240p for one player and 480p for more.
- **16:9 looks narrow in PCSX2,** because PCSX2 shows it at 4:3. A TV set to 16:9 stretches it to the right shape.
- **One player stops at "Linking with other systems...":** Four Swords waits for a link partner, so single player needs its own work later.

I haven't looked at Four Swords' own scrolling or sprite code yet. What follows comes from the Minish Cap engine it shares (`reference/tmc`), where the 240×160 screen size is used in 16 files.

**1. Renderer (contained work).** mGBA's software renderer has 240×160 built in: line buffers, sprite clipping and window ranges. Making the width and height variables and the output buffers bigger is mechanical. The GS side is trivial: a 320×240 texture for one player, or 640×240 per player for two. The renderer also costs more as the area grows: two 640×240 screens are 8× the pixels of two 240×160 ones. Drawing is already the main cost per frame.

**2. GBA hardware limits the extra area runs into.**
- **Background maps** are at most 512×512 pixels and wrap around. 320×240 fits. A 640-wide view is wider than the largest map, so the left and right edges would show the same tiles.
- **Sprite positions** are 9 bits across (0–511) and 8 bits down (0–255). Anything past x 511 wraps to the left side. For 640-wide screens, the port would need its own wider sprite coordinates, set where the game writes its sprite table.
- **Window, mosaic and rotated-background registers** have similar 8-bit screen ranges. Effects like light circles and transitions use them.

**3. The game itself (most of the work):**
- **Tile streaming:** the engine writes only the map tiles near the visible screen, a column or row at a time as the camera moves. A wider view shows tiles that were never written.
- **Camera limits:** the camera is clamped to room edges using 240 and 160. Many rooms are about one screen in size. A bigger view would show past the room edge unless there's a fill or a black border.
- **Off-screen culling:** enemies and objects outside 240×160 (plus a margin) aren't drawn, and some aren't updated. Widening this could change gameplay, such as when enemies wake up.
- **HUD and menus** (hearts, rupees, pause, "P1 PAUSE!") sit at fixed positions for 240×160. They need re-anchoring to the new edges.
- **Fixed-size screens** like the title, file select, cutscenes and full-screen effects need a border or their own handling.

**4. Our code base makes it harder.** Most Four Swords code is still assembly translated to C, not readable C. The 240 and 160 values are buried as constants inside that translated code, so each place has to be found and patched there. Or the functions involved get decompiled first, which is the slow part.

**Suggested order:**
1. **Renderer with a bigger area**, run on unchanged game code. This shows what goes wrong where (wrapped maps, missing tiles, culled sprites) without changing the game.
2. **One player at 320×240 first.** It stays within the GBA's map and sprite limits, so only streaming, camera, culling and HUD need changes.
3. **640×240 after that.** It also needs the wider sprite coordinates and a way past the 512-pixel map wrap.

The DSi Anniversary Edition's wider screen (`reference/dsi`) may show how Nintendo handled HUD placement and room edges, and could be worth a look before designing step 3.

Step 1 is a reasonable first experiment: probably a day or two of work. It would give screenshots showing how much each problem actually matters. Should I start there?

## Claude

Step 1 makes the renderer draw a bigger area from the game's unchanged video memory and registers, then shows what appears in the extra part. No game code changes.

**What changes**

1. **mGBA renderer** ([src/ps2/mgba](src/ps2/mgba)): 240 and 160 are fixed constants in `interface.h`, used in 6 renderer files (35 places in `video-software.c`). I'd turn them into a view width and height set at startup. The per-line buffers would be sized for the largest view, 640×240. Two rules need adjusting, not just the size:
   - **Sprite wraparound:** today a sprite at x ≥ 240 that ends before 512 is treated as hanging off the left edge. Below the screen it's y ≥ 160 that ends before 228. With a bigger view, those positions are on screen, so the test moves to the new width and height.
   - **Window registers:** a game sets "right edge 240" or "bottom 160" to mean the whole screen. Taken literally, that clips everything past 240×160. I'd treat 240 and 160 as "to the edge of the view". It's a guess that may need cases.
2. **Video output** ([video.c](src/ps2/video.c)):
   - Pixel buffers become 640 wide (still 256 tall); texture sizes follow the view.
   - GS memory: two 480p frame buffers (2.4 MB) plus two 640×240 textures (1.2 MB) fit in the GS's 4 MB, with little left over.
   - Layouts: one player at 320×240 fills the 240p frame at 1:1 (2× in 480p). Two players at 640×240 each fill the 480p frame exactly, one above the other.
3. **The option:** `make -f Makefile.ps2 VIEW=wide` (or similar), off by default, alongside `VIDEO_MODE`. Without it, the output stays exactly as now.

**What it shows**

The GBA picture stays at the top-left of the bigger view, and the extra area is to its right and below. That's where the problems show up:
- **Map tiles never written:** the map wraps, or shows stale tiles from earlier rooms.
- **Room edges:** beyond the room there's no fill, so whatever the map holds there appears.
- **Culled objects:** enemies and objects past the old screen edge are missing, or freeze when they come into view.
- **Hidden sprites:** sprites the game "hides" by parking them at x 240 or y 160 may now appear. On the GBA, that's just off screen.
- **Fixed-size screens:** the title, file select and lobby show leftover tiles in the extra area.

**Checks**
- **Same picture where it overlaps:** with the option on, the top-left 240×160 of each screen should match the normal build's frame. Any difference is a renderer bug, not a game problem.
- **Screenshots:** frame dumps at the title, file select, lobby, the stage, and some frames with the camera moving. Two players at 640×240, one player at 320×240. I'd send you the set with notes on what each shows.
- **Usual run checks:** no TLB misses, `make compare` OK, a walkthrough entry, and a commit.

**Cost and limits**
- **Speed:** drawing two 640×240 screens is about 8 times the pixels of two 240×160 ones. Drawing already took about 4.2M EE cycles per screen out of 4.9M per frame. Wide two-player would run at only a few frames per second in PCSX2, which is fine for screenshots but not for play. Fixing that is a separate job: drawing on the GS instead of in software.
- **Camera:** for step 1 the game camera isn't moved or centred, so each player's Link stays where they'd be on a 240×160 screen, top-left. Centring comes with the game-side changes.
- **Map width:** at 640 wide, the right 128 pixels repeat the left of the 512-pixel map. That's expected, and the screenshots will show it.

Estimate: about a day for the renderer and output, plus the screenshot run. Shall I go ahead?

## Claude

Step 1 is done: with `make -f Makefile.ps2 WIDE_VIEW=1`, the renderer draws 320×240 for one player and 640×240 each for two, from the unchanged game. I sent three images: the two-player PCSX2 screen, frame dumps at the title, Choose a Stage and the stage while walking, and the single-player screen at the lobby. Committed as `b1b175f`; the matching build still reports OK.

**Check:** at each dump frame, the wide build also drew the normal 240×160 picture from the same state. All 10 dumps (both players, five moments) match the wide frame's top-left 240×160 exactly. So the renderer changes don't alter the normal picture.

**What the extra area shows:**
- **Backgrounds repeat every 256 pixels across.** Four Swords' maps here are 256 wide, so the room and the HUD (hearts, rupee counter) appear about two and a half times on a 640-wide screen. The repeat is the map wrapping, not more of the room. This is the main problem: the game only keeps a screen's worth of map, so real extra content has to come from the game side.
- **Below line 160:** map rows the game never fills. In the stage that's black with stray tiles; on the title it's tile data shown as garbage.
- **Sprites the GBA keeps out of sight appear:** a second copy of the switches below the screen, and a "YOU / P1" marker parked at x 250 in the lobby.
- **Speed:** wide two-player drawing takes about 4× the frame time; PCSX2 ran at about 12 fps.

**Problems found on the way:**
- **Build bug (fixed):** mGBA's objects weren't rebuilt when its headers changed. After the struct change, the stage drew with no backgrounds until I found it. The Makefile now rebuilds them.

## Claude

Moving drawing to the GS means rebuilding the GBA's picture-drawing hardware out of GS primitives. The EE would only turn video memory, palettes and sprite tables into textures and draw lists; the GS draws the pixels. That removes the software renderer's cost: today it's about 4 million EE cycles per screen, nearly a whole 60 Hz frame (4.9 million).

The planning doc already expected this ("GS tile rendering later if too slow"). The HAL's `gpu_gs.c` (about 3,900 lines) already does the hardest similar job, drawing the PS1's palette-based 4- and 8-bit textures on the GS. Its palette uploads, texture cache and blend settings are good patterns to follow.

**What has to be built**

1. **Tiles to GS textures.** GBA video memory holds 8×8 tiles in 4-bit (16 colours) or 8-bit (256 colours). Each frame, the EE would copy changed tiles into GS textures of the same formats, laid out 32 tiles per row. The GS's largest texture is 1024×1024, so tiles can't simply be stacked in one column. That's at most 96 KB per instance per frame, and less if only changed tiles are copied.
2. **Palettes.** The 512 GBA colours (15-bit) become GS colour tables (32-bit), with colour 0 of each 16-colour set transparent via alpha. The GS's alpha test then drops transparent pixels.
3. **Tile backgrounds (mode 0), the main case.**
   - Each visible map entry becomes an 8×8 textured rectangle. Flips are swapped texture coordinates, and the palette is chosen per rectangle.
   - That's about 650 rectangles per layer and up to 4 layers per screen, a light load for the GS.
   - Scrolling is an offset, and map wraparound is handled when building the list.
   - Rectangles sharing a palette should be batched, since switching palettes costs GS commands.
4. **Sprites:**
   - sizes 8 to 64 pixels;
   - 1D and 2D tile layouts;
   - flips and 16- or 256-colour palettes;
   - rotated and scaled sprites as transformed quads using the sprite's matrix.
5. **Layer order.** The list is drawn back to front: for priority 3 down to 0, the backgrounds at that priority, then the sprites at that priority. Sprites go in reverse table order, so lower-numbered ones end up on top, as on the GBA.
6. **Rotating/scaling backgrounds (modes 1 and 2), if Four Swords uses them.** The map is drawn as tiles with the background's matrix applied to the vertices. Wraparound needs extra copies of the map.
7. **Windows.** Window 0 and window 1 rectangles become GS scissor rectangles: a layer is drawn once per window region that shows it. The sprite window, where sprite shapes act as a mask, needs a mask pass using the GS's destination-alpha test.
8. **Blending (the hard part):**
   - The GBA computes A×eva + B×evb, clamped. The GS can only do (A−B)×C+D in one pass, so it's exact only when eva+evb = 16. Other cases need two passes or an approximation.
   - The GBA also blends only where the pixel underneath belongs to a chosen "second target" layer. The GS has nothing like that, so it would be approximated. The HAL's PS1 blending has the same kind of limits.
   - Fading to white or black (`BLDY`) only affects the chosen layers, so it's applied per layer as a blend.
9. **Mosaic** is probably rare. It would start approximated or left out.
10. **Per-scanline effects** (registers changed partway down the screen) aren't supported today either, since the picture is drawn after the frame. That stays the same.

**GS memory.** The 4 MB holds the 480p frame buffers (2.4 MB) plus about 100 KB of tiles and palettes per instance, so four players fit. It's tight with the wide view, but that could use one buffer, or 16-bit colour.

**How to check it.** The software renderer stays in the build as the reference. At chosen frames, the same state is drawn both ways: the GS picture is read back and compared pixel by pixel with mGBA's. That gives an exact difference count per frame, much like the wide-view check, and shows exactly which feature is wrong.

**Suggested order**
1. **Survey first.** Log which video features Four Swords actually uses across the recordings: display modes, rotated backgrounds or sprites, windows, blend modes, mosaic. That decides how much of 6–9 is needed. It's cheapest to log in `mgba_run`, which plays the same recordings. Maybe half a day.
2. **Backgrounds and sprites, no effects,** with the comparison running. That should already draw most of the game correctly.
3. **Windows and blending,** working down the frames that still differ.
4. **Then:** four players at full speed, and the wide view, which becomes cheap once the GS draws it.

As a rough estimate, the survey plus step 2 is a few days of work, and step 3 depends on what the survey finds. The new bug from the wide-view work (the bad instruction around frame 1770) is still open. It's separate from this and can be fixed before or alongside it.

First explain blending and scanline effects in more detail

## Claude

Both are GBA features that don't map directly onto the GS. Here's how each works, what the port does today, and how the GS version would handle it.

## Blending

**What the GBA does.** Three registers control it:
- `BLDCNT` picks an effect (none, alpha blend, brighten or darken). It also has two layer lists: the **first targets** (any of BG0–3, sprites, backdrop) and the **second targets**.
- `BLDALPHA` holds two weights, eva and evb, each 0–16 (in sixteenths).
- `BLDY` holds the brighten/darken amount, evy (0–16).

The GBA keeps the top two layers for every pixel: the visible one (A) and the one directly under it (B).
- **Alpha blend:** applies only if A is a first target and B is a second target. The result is min(31, A×eva/16 + B×evb/16) per 5-bit channel. Otherwise A shows unblended.
- **Semi-transparent sprites** (a per-sprite flag) blend with whatever is below, if it's a second target, even when the selected effect isn't alpha. That's how shadows, ghosts and glows are usually done.
- **Brighten:** A + (31−A)×evy/16. **Darken:** A − A×evy/16. Both apply only where A is a first target. Fades to white or black are usually this, with every layer as a first target.
- **Windows** can switch effects off per region (a bit in `WININ`/`WINOUT`).

**What the GS can do.** One blend formula: ((A − B) × C) / 128 + D.
- A, B and D can each be the colour being drawn (Cs), the colour already in the frame buffer (Cd), or 0.
- C can be the drawn alpha, the frame buffer's alpha, or a fixed value.
- Results above 255 can be clamped.

**How each GBA case would map:**

| GBA case | GS approach | Exact? |
|---|---|---|
| Alpha with eva + evb = 16 (the usual 50/50, 75/25) | One pass: (Cs − Cd) × eva + Cd | Yes |
| Alpha with other sums (e.g. 16 + 16, an additive glow) | Two passes over the same shape: first scale the frame buffer by evb (Cd − Cd×(1−evb)), then add Cs×eva | Yes, at the cost of drawing it twice |
| Darken | A second pass on the layer's shape: Cd × (1 − evy) | Yes |
| Brighten | The formula can't add a constant white, so: mark the layer's pixels, then draw a white rectangle that blends only there | Needs a marking pass |
| Whole-screen fade (every layer a first target) | One full-screen rectangle at the end | Yes |
| "Only blend if the layer under it is a second target" | Each layer writes a flag into the frame buffer's alpha bit (1 for second target, 0 otherwise). The blended layer is drawn twice: once blended where the flag is set, once opaque where it isn't, using the GS's destination-alpha test. | Yes |

Layers are drawn back to front, so the frame buffer's flag always describes the layer directly underneath, which is exactly what the GBA checks. The catch is that brighten's marking pass also needs the alpha bit, so those two jobs have to take turns. That's doable because each layer is drawn and finished one at a time.

**Rounding.** The GBA works in 5 bits per channel and the GS in 8. Without care, blended pixels come out one or two levels different from mGBA. The pixel comparison would either allow that tolerance for blended pixels, or the formula would be chosen to round the same way.

So blending can be made exact or very close, but each effect costs extra passes and careful ordering. That's why the survey matters: it'll show which of these cases Four Swords actually uses.

## Scanline effects

**What they are.** The GBA draws the screen one line at a time while the game runs, and the game can change video registers between lines:
- **HBlank DMA:** a DMA channel set to repeat every line copies the next entry of a table into a register. Common uses:
  - background scroll per line (heat shimmer, water wobble, parallax layers);
  - the window's left and right edges per line (circle "iris" wipes, spotlights);
  - colours per line.
- **HBlank or VCount interrupts:** game code runs at a chosen line. The usual case is a split screen, such as a HUD with different scroll or mode from the play area.

**What the port does today.** The game runs a whole frame, and only then is the picture drawn, using the registers as they are at the end of the frame. Per-line changes are lost, and only the last value counts. The DMA emulation in [io.c](src/ps2/io.c) only runs immediate and VBlank DMAs; HBlank DMAs (start timing 2) never run. So any such effect already draws wrong today, with the software renderer too. For example, an iris wipe would show one window width for every line.

**How to support it (the same idea for either renderer):**
1. **Capture per-line values.** An HBlank DMA's table is already in memory before the frame is drawn: entry *y* is the register value for line *y*. When drawing, the port reads the table instead of running the DMA. Mid-frame interrupt code is harder; it would need the game's writes recorded with the line they happen on.
2. **Draw with them:**
   - **Software renderer (works today):** mGBA's renderer was built for this. Write the register before drawing each line. Cheap to add.
   - **GS:** split each layer into horizontal bands where its state doesn't change. A per-line scroll becomes up to 160 one-line bands, which is still little work for the GS.
   - **GS window edges per line:** an iris becomes 160 one-line scissor rectangles, or a shape built from triangles.

Finding out whether Four Swords uses these is part of the survey: log any HBlank DMA or HBlank/VCount interrupt it sets up. If it does (iris transitions are likely, since the Minish Cap engine does them), I'd add the table reading to the software renderer first. That fixes the current output and gives the GS version a correct reference to compare against.

## Claude

A GS renderer only needs a small part of the GBA's video features, and in the stage itself almost none of the hard ones. The survey covered the intro (boot through file select and name entry to Choose a Stage, 1,700 frames) and session 1 (one full stage, 44,522 frames), with two linked GBAs. I sent a sheet showing where each effect first appears.

**What Four Swords uses**
- **Display mode 0 only:** four 16-colour tile backgrounds. There are no rotating/scaling backgrounds, no bitmap modes and no 256-colour tiles. Some screens set the mosaic bits, but the mosaic size stays 0, so nothing visible happens.
- **Sprites:**
  - rotating/scaling sprites in the stage, including some double-size ones (the item-get around frame 28,900);
  - a different tile layout for sprites (2D mapping) on Choose a Stage;
  - no see-through sprites, no sprite window, no sprite mosaic and no 256-colour sprites.
- **Windows:** window 0 only, never window 1.

**Blending:** almost all full-screen fades, which are the easy case for the GS.

| Effect | Where | GS difficulty |
|---|---|---|
| Fade to black or white, all layers | Stage start and end | Easy: one rectangle over the screen |
| BG2 blended over BG3, 12/16 + 8/16 (sum 20, not 16) | File select, name entry | Needs the two-pass method |
| BG1 blended over everything, 4/16 + 12/16 | The A Link to the Past / Four Swords choice fading in | One pass |
| Brighten BG2 only | The A Link to the Past title fading | Needs the marking pass |

**Effects that change partway down the screen:** two, both short transitions, and both driven by an HBlank DMA reading a table. That's the easy kind to support, because the table is in memory when the frame is drawn.
1. **The diagonal wipe into and out of a stage** (frames 1701–1752 and 44,297–44,415): window 0's left and right edges change on every line, and the area outside is darkened.
2. **The game-choice transition** (frames 846–938): BG3's horizontal scroll changes per line.

The game also has an interrupt at line 0 on all the time, but it doesn't change the picture mid-frame.

**What this means for the plan**
- The GS renderer's core is 16-colour tile backgrounds plus sprites, including rotating/scaling ones. That covers the whole stage apart from its fades.
- The two-pass and marking-pass blend methods are needed only on menus. They can come after the stage is right.
- The two per-line effects are currently wrong in the port, even with the software renderer, since the port ignores HBlank DMAs. Reading the DMA table at draw time would fix both renderers, and it's a small change.

This only covers the menus and one stage (the Chambers of Insight). Other stages, bosses, and the pause, results and game-over screens weren't recorded, so more recordings would need the same survey. Running it takes about a minute.

## Claude

The GS renderer now draws Four Swords' screens the same as the software renderer, at about a quarter of the cost. It's switched on with `make -f Makefile.ps2 GS_RENDER=1`; the software renderer is still the default.

**Comparison:** I ran the 2-player intro replay and compared the GS output with the software renderer pixel by pixel. I read the GS picture back from the same game state at 34 frames per screen: the lobby, the window wipe that opens Choose a Stage, the stage map, and the stage itself.
- **33 of 34 identical:** 0 pixels differ.
- **The lobby:** 3,261 pixels are one colour level off in its blended background, and none by more. The GS has to round the two blended colours separately, while mGBA rounds their sum once.
- **Speed:** both screens take about 1.5M EE cycles a frame, against about 6M for the software renderer, out of 4.9M per 60 Hz frame. Drawing is no longer what limits the frame rate. With the GS renderer, PCSX2 ran this 2-player build at full speed.
- **No TLB misses.**

**What it draws:** everything the survey found: tile backgrounds, sprites (including rotated/scaled ones), window 0 with per-line edges, fades, and alpha blending.

**Per-line effects (before the GS work):** the HBlank DMA effects weren't showing in either renderer, because the port never ran the game's VCount interrupt, which starts the DMA. It now does, so both renderers show the window wipe. The wipe matches mGBA exactly for its first frames. Later in it, edges and line 0 differ slightly, probably from a GBA lag frame the port doesn't reproduce; I haven't confirmed that. The interrupt also runs the sound mixer every frame. The port has no sound yet, so that call is skipped for now; it's marked as a shortcut.

**Bugs fixed along the way:**
- **Palettes:** a 4-bit texture loads only 16 palette entries at a time, so each 16-colour palette now has its own CLUT.
- **Colour conversion:** mGBA converts 5-bit colour to 8-bit with the low bits filled in; I had used a plain shift.
- **Flipped tiles:** they read one column of the next tile, because the GS samples at a pixel's corner.
- **Rectangles:** a GIF packet format mix-up meant the fade, window mask and backdrop rectangles were garbage.
- **DMA source 0:** the game briefly starts a DMA from address 0, which caused TLB misses. Both renderers now skip it.

**Not covered yet:**
- **Untested screens:** the GS renderer hasn't been tried with 4 players, the wide view (it refuses to build with it), or screens outside these recordings, such as other stages, bosses and the results screen.
- **Unimplemented features:** mosaic, window 1 and the sprite window. Brighten/darken currently assumes every layer is affected, which is true of all the fades recorded.
- **Unreached transition:** the per-line BG3 scroll in the game-choice transition isn't reached in this build, because it boots straight into Four Swords.

Committed in three steps (`5e89c05`, `8eb3d0f`, `bad78b8`), with walkthrough Steps 32–34.

Next could be making the GS renderer the default and checking 4 players at full speed. The open bad-instruction bug from the walking replay is still worth fixing first.

2. Key Technical Concepts:
   - **Instance memory:** copy-swap. One live block; saved copies at 0x01900000 + i MB.
   - **gsKit video modes:**
     - `Mode`, `Interlace`, `Field`, `Width`, `Height` are set before `gsKit_init_screen`.
     - DISPLAY1/2: MAGH = DW / fbw - 1, centred (taken from the HAL's display_ps2.c).
     - 720p: a 640x720 buffer doubled horizontally, CT16.
     - 16:9: widths in square pixels × 640/854.
   - **PCSX2 aspect:** the user's ini says 16:9. pshot.sh passes `--set "AspectRatio=${ASPECT:-4:3}"`.
   - **mGBA renderer changes:**
     - The screen size is the runtime variables `ps2_view_w/h`.
     - The Makefile now rebuilds mGBA objects when its headers change.
   - **Interrupt dispatch:**
     - The game's VCount handler table entry is `INTR_TABLE+8`; VBlank is `+4`.
     - `process_dma_request` (line 0) starts the HBlank DMA. `sub_0800B7FC` (line 32) runs the sound mixer, `sub_081339D4`, which is native ARM and not translated.
     - The table holds PS2 addresses of native C functions.
   - **HBlank DMA:** line y uses table entry y-1. A source below 0x02000000 is skipped.
   - **GS renderer basics:**
     - Textures: a T4 texture of 256x768 (BG tiles in rows 0-511, OBJ tiles in rows 512-767).
     - Palettes: 32 CLUTs of 8x2 CT32, 256 bytes apart, loaded with CLD=4.
     - Colour expansion matches mGBA: `(c<<3)|(c>>2)`.
     - TFX MODULATE; the vertex alpha carries the second-target flag.
     - Alpha test GEQUAL 0x40.
   - **GS sampling:** the GS samples at a pixel's top-left corner. A flipped tile's UV start is (u+8)*16-1 and its end is u*16.
   - **Window 0:**
     - Default: an alpha mask with FBMSK 0x00FFFFFF, then DATE.
     - While blending: scissor rectangles. A per-line or wrapping window with blending isn't supported.
   - **Fades:**
     - Darken: ALPHA(2,1,2,1,evy*8).
     - Brighten: ALPHA(0,1,2,1,evy*8) with a white Cs.
   - **Alpha blending:** four passes for a first-target layer:
     1. FBMSK on alpha, DATE pass: ALPHA(2,1,2,1,(16-evb)*8).
     2. ALPHA(0,2,2,1,eva*8), with COLCLAMP.
     3. Opaque with DATM=0.
     4. The layer's own flag, written to alpha only.
   - **PACKED GIF tags:** register formats differ by register. Untextured rectangles must use A+D.
   - **Readback:** taken from tp-ps2's download_rows (originally from the HAL). The DMA goes straight to dst, followed by InvalidDCache.
   - **EE heap:** about 1.6 MB left. gsKit pools are shrunk with `gsKit_init_global_custom(64K,16K)`.

3. Files and Code Sections:
   - **src/ps2/video.c**
     - Mode table `sModes`:
       - 240p: NTSC, 320x240, scale 1
       - 480i: 640x480, scale 2
       - 480p: 640x480, scale 2
       - 480p 16:9: aw 854, scale 3
       - 720p: 640x720, CT16, scale 4
     - `ps2_video_mode = VIDEO_MODE` (auto: 240p for one player, 480p otherwise).
     - `place()`: one player at the mode's scale, fitted to the view. Two players at 1:1, stacked with no gap, centred: `*y = (ah - 2 * *h)/2 + i * *h`. Three or four players in a 2x2 grid.
     - Pixel buffers: `ps2_view_w/h`, `sTexW`, and `sPixelPool[2*640*240]` with `PIXELS(i) = sPixelPool + i*sTexW*PS2_VIEW_MAX_H`.
     - Wide-view check pass: `_gba` dumps.
     - `render()` returns the number of active HBlank DMA channels. `hblank_dma(r,y)` applies table entries; at y=160 it writes entry 159 into the I/O register.
     - HBlank-DMA frame dumps (24 at most, every 4th frame).
     - GS mode:
       - `ps2_gsr_init`; `tex.Vram = ps2_gsr_target(i)` and `TBW = sTexW/64`.
       - No texture upload.
       - Before `gsKit_clear`: `gsKit_setactive`, `gsKit_set_scissor(GS_SCISSOR_RESET)`, `gsKit_set_test(GS_ATEST_OFF)`.
       - At dump frames: the software render, the readback, a pixel comparison logged as "N pixels differ…, M by more than one level", and both images written as `_gs.ppm` and plain.
   - **src/ps2/gsrender.c** (new)
     - Covers: upload, put_clut, tex0, tex_rect (REGLIST of 6 registers), flat (A+D), draw_mask, in_regions/draw_layer (blending), draw_bg, draw_objs (affine sprites as triangles via the inverse matrix), fade_fn, win0h_lines, ps2_gsr_init/target/draw/read.
     - `FULL()` guards the packet (DRAW_QW 16000).
   - **src/ps2/frame.c**
     - `ps2_vblank_wait` now raises the VCount interrupts after VBlank: each line at most once per frame, in line order.

## Claude

The GS renderer is now the default, and 4 players show as four 240x160 screens at 1:1 in a 2x2 block centred in the 640x480 frame. But 4 players still run at only 30 fps. Committed as `09181c6`; `make compare` reports OK.

**Default and layout**
- Builds use the GS renderer unless you pass `GS_RENDER=0`. Builds with `WIDE_VIEW` still use the software renderer, because the GS renderer doesn't do the wider view yet.
- The block is 480x320, with P1 and P2 on top and P3 and P4 below ([video.c](src/ps2/video.c), `place()`). Before, each screen was scaled up to fill a quarter of the frame. The screenshot is attached.

**Speed**
4 players first cost 4.6M EE cycles a frame to draw (about 1.1M per screen), against 4.9M available per 60 fps frame. Most of that was building the GS draw commands each frame, so I made two changes in [gsrender.c](src/ps2/gsrender.c):
- Background tiles that are fully transparent are no longer drawn.
- A blended background used to have its tile list rebuilt for each of its four drawing passes. It is now built once and reused.

| | Before | After |
|---|---|---|
| 4 screens | 4.6M | 2.6M |
| 2 screens | 1.5M | 1.2M |

The pictures didn't change. In the 2-player replay, all 34 compared frames matched the software renderer pixel for pixel. That run didn't happen to compare a lobby frame, the one that used to be one colour level off. In the 4-player run, every difference is the same one-level blend rounding as before.

**Why it's still 30 fps**
The game code for four players, plus copying each player's memory in and out every frame, takes 3.9M cycles on its own. That leaves about 1M for drawing four screens. Getting to full speed needs work on both sides:
- the remaining drawing cost: about 0.3M per screen goes to rearranging the graphics data into a GS texture each frame;
- the per-player memory copy, about 387 KB for each player switch.

**Errors in the 4-player run**
The 4-player run logs 50 TLB misses in `gs_sub_08003870`, where file-select code reads through a null animation pointer. This is the known open bug from Step 26: it depends on the save file and happens with one player too. Players 3 and 4 have no recorded inputs, so they sit on the file select, where it shows up. The rendering changes didn't cause it; it appeared before them too.

`docs/Running Walkthrough.md` Step 35 and the conversation archive are updated.

**Next steps, for you to pick:**
- Fix the file-select null pointer.
- Work toward 60 fps with 4 players: the texture rearranging and the per-player memory copy.
- Look at the earlier bad-instruction crash around frame 1770.

# Shared world for split-screen: outline and speed estimate

**The short answer:** most of the speed-up would come from running the game once instead of four times, not from rendering. I estimate a 4-player frame would drop from about 6.5M EE cycles to roughly 3.2–3.8M. The budget at 60 fps is 4.9M, so 4 players would fit. Rendering alone would only get about 25–35% cheaper.

## Where the time goes now (4 players, measured)

| Cost per frame | EE cycles |
|---|---|
| Game code ×4, plus copying each player's memory in and out at every switch | 3.9M |
| Rendering, about 0.65M per screen: | 2.6M |
| – rearranging the graphics memory into a GS texture | 0.3M per screen |
| – building the draw commands | ~0.35M per screen |
| **Total** (60 fps budget: 4.9M) | **6.5M** |

All four game copies simulate the same world in lockstep: every enemy, object and all four Links. Each copy only differs in which player it follows. So most of that 3.9M is the same work done four times. I haven't timed the memory copying apart from the game code yet; that's the first thing to measure.

## Outline

**Phase 0: measure and map.** This doesn't change the game.
1. Time the memory copying separately from the game code. Inside the 3.9M, that split decides how much the cheap step 4 below gains.
2. Log and decode the link packet: 12 halfwords per player per frame. The planning doc's Phase 5 depends on the cable carrying little more than inputs.
3. Compare the four copies' memory at the same frame. Bytes that differ are per-player state; everything else is the shared world. The copy-swap blocks at 0x01900000 + i MB make this a small tool. I expect it to find:
   - the camera and background scroll;
   - the background tile maps around each camera;
   - the sprite list the game builds for the GBA's sprite hardware;
   - the HUD and menus;
   - the "which player am I" ID;
   - possibly some sprite graphics loaded per player.
4. Find every place the game reads its own player number (the link status register). Those are the branches where "this GBA's player" matters.

**Phase 1: run the world once, keep the per-player parts.** This is the incremental step, under an `FS_SHARED_WORLD` option that breaks GBA matching on purpose.
5. Split the game frame into two parts:
   - the world update, run once;
   - the per-player part, run once per player with that player's small state block swapped in: input, camera, HUD, sprite list, background tile maps.
   
   The memory copying then shrinks from roughly 387 KB per switch to a few KB.
6. Replace the link exchange with direct reads of the shared input array. Every player's inputs are already in the same memory.
7. Check it against the current 4-instance build with the same scripted inputs: compare each player's screen frame by frame (the GS readback check already does this) and compare world memory.

**Phase 2: render from shared graphics.**
8. Upload the tile graphics and palettes once per frame instead of four times. That saves about 0.9M.
9. Per camera, draw only what differs: background tile maps, scroll, sprite list, windows and fades. The GS renderer already takes these per screen, so it changes little.

**Phase 3: audio.** One sound mixer fed by the shared world, instead of four.

## Estimate (4 players, per frame)

| | Now | Shared world |
|---|---|---|
| World update | ~3.9M combined | ~0.9–1.2M (once) |
| Per-player game work ×4 | (included above) | ~0.4–0.6M |
| Memory copying | (included above) | ~0.05M |
| Graphics upload | 1.2M | 0.3M |
| Draw commands ×4 | 1.4M | ~1.4M |
| **Total** | **6.5M (30 fps)** | **~3.2–3.8M (60 fps)** |

- **Game side:** about 3–4× faster. This is where the gain is.
- **Rendering:** about 2.6M down to about 1.7M. Each camera still sees different tiles, so the draw commands stay per player.
- **Uncertainty:**
  - The per-player share is a guess until steps 1 and 3 measure it.
  - If the game reloads sprite graphics per player, those can't be shared, which reduces the upload saving.
- **Other routes to 60 fps without a shared world:** cutting the remaining texture-rearranging and memory-copy costs. Those can only win back part of the 1.6M over budget, because the four game copies stay.

## Risks
- **Hidden player-only code:** code that assumes "the local player" in places Phase 0 doesn't catch. Step 7's check is there for this.
- **Translated code:** functions not yet decompiled are still auto-translated, so splitting the frame update can mean decompiling the main loop and the per-player HUD/camera code first.
- **More than 4 players:** the shared world makes this easier later, because per-player arrays get sized by one constant.

I'd start with Phase 0 steps 1 and 3. They take about a session and settle both the estimate and whether this plan works at all.

## Claude

Step 1 changes the estimate: almost all of the game's time goes to copying each player's memory in and out, not to running the game four times.

I wrote the plan into Phase 5 of [Planning Doc.md](docs/Planning Doc.md), with phases 0–3, steps 1–10 and a checkbox for each, and I'll update it as we go. Step 1 is checked off with its numbers, and Step 36 of the walkthrough has the details. Committed as `40bbdaa`; `make compare` reports OK.

**What I measured:** the 10-second cost line now separates the player memory switches from the game code ([tlb.c](src/ps2/tlb.c)). The game code is everything else in the game's share, including link exchange, input and saves. Cycles per frame, out of 4.9M at 60 fps:

| Run | Game's share | Memory switches | Game code |
|---|---|---|---|
| 4 players, lobby and file select | 3.92M | 3.57M | 0.35M |
| 2 players, lobby | 2.42M | 1.78M | 0.64M |
| 2 players, stage, idle after the recording ends | 1.84M | 1.78M | 0.05M |

- **Switches:** each one copies 387 KB out and 387 KB in, about 0.9M cycles per player per frame. They take about 90% of the game's share.
- **Game code:** small in every scene measured. My estimate assumed the four simulations were the expensive part, and they aren't.
- **Not measured:** a busy 4-player stage, because there's no 4-player input recording yet. The stage numbers come from players standing idle, so real gameplay will cost more.

**What this means for the plan:**
- A shared world would still be fast, mostly because it removes the switches. Running the game once saves little on top of that.
- Making the switches cheap would reach 60 fps with 4 players on its own: about 2.6M rendering plus 0.35M game code, with no game changes. Ways to do that include copying only the memory that changed, using faster copies, or not copying at all.
- The shared world's other reasons (one camera per player into one world, easier support for more than 4 players) don't depend on speed.

I'd do steps 2 and 3 next as planned (decode the link packet and compare the players' memory). Step 3 also shows which memory differs between players, and that would tell us how little a cheap switch needs to copy.

## Claude

Steps 2 and 3 are done and both support the shared-world plan. The link cable carries only inputs, and the two players' copies of the game differ in about 13 KB of their 480 KB of memory. Both results are in the plan ([Planning Doc.md](docs/Planning Doc.md), Phase 5) and walkthrough Step 37, committed as `e006786` (`make compare` reports OK).

Both come from the 2-player replay, which covers the lobby, Choose a Stage, the stage, and P1 opening the pause menu. I used temporary logging and memory dumps, and removed them afterwards.

**Step 2, the link packet:** I logged all 7,656 packets the two players sent. Each is 12 halfwords per player per frame:
- a frame counter and status byte, then a checksum;
- 20 bytes of game data: a byte naming the current screen, that player's buttons for the last 5 frames (resent as a safety margin), another frame counter, and 6 bytes that were always zero.

No world state is ever sent. Each GBA works out the whole world on its own from everyone's inputs. The planning doc's old condition for a shared world ("only if the cable carries little more than inputs") is met. Screens the replay doesn't reach are untested: the shop, results, item choice, and any 4-player stage.

**Step 3, what differs between players:** at a stage frame where each camera followed its own Link, about 13 KB differ, in 31 of the 120 4 KB pages:

| Area | Size | What's there |
|---|---|---|
| Main RAM | ~10 KB | Largest block (~6 KB) is likely a background map around each player's camera. Also each player's own save data, text boxes, a few small per-player records, link state |
| Fast RAM | ~0.7 KB | Scroll registers, two ~300-byte blocks that look like sprite lists, a few entity bytes |
| Video memory | ~4.4 KB | Background maps, 128 bytes of tiles, 35 bytes of the sprite table |

The world itself is identical in both: enemies, objects and room data, plus all palettes and every sprite tile. So in Phase 2 the graphics can be uploaded once for all players.

**Cheaper switches can't skip memory yet.** Copying only the 31 differing pages would be far less work. But it isn't possible while every copy of the game still runs the world, because the shared pages would get each frame's world update once per player. It only works once the world runs once, which is Phase 1.

**Next is step 4:** finding every place the game uses its own player number. The number arrives through the link status register, which only [io.c](src/ps2/io.c) and [link.c](src/ps2/link.c) answer. I'd log where the game reads it and where it stores it, then look for code that reads that stored copy. Those are the "this is me" branches that Phase 1 has to make per player.

Phase 0 is finished: the game uses its own player number in 18 functions, plus 5 more that go through a pointer to the player's record. Steps 2–4 are recorded in the plan ([Planning Doc.md](docs/Planning Doc.md), Phase 5) and walkthrough Steps 37–38. Committed as `a6b2a24`; `make compare` reports OK.

**Where the number lives:** the game reads its player number from the link hardware once, when linking, and stores it in one byte at 0x03000414. The symbol file calls that byte `gLCDRegisterBuffer`, which is a wrong name. A second function then keeps a pointer to that player's own record.

**How I found the readers:** I added a `--reads ADDR` option to the mGBA runner. It logs every instruction that reads a given address, with its caller. I replayed the recorded 2-player session 1 with it, about 44,500 frames covering the lobby, one whole stage and the return to Choose a Stage.

- **The player number byte:** 48 read sites in 18 functions. They fall into three kinds:
  - "Is this mine?" checks on entities and sounds.
  - Indexes into per-player arrays: buttons, the link buffer, player records.
  - The HUD, menus and file select.
- **The record pointer:** 5 functions, mostly in the file select.

These are the "this is me" branches Phase 1 has to run once per player.

**Not covered yet:**
- **Scenes session 1 doesn't reach:** other stages, bosses, results, the shop.
- **Code the watch can't see:** ARM-mode code, and Thumb code running from RAM.
- **Copies of the number:** any copy kept in another variable. None turned up at the sites seen.

**Phase 0 in short:**
- The cable carries only inputs.
- The players differ in about 13 KB of memory.
- About 23 functions know which player they belong to.
- Copying player memory in and out, not running the game four times, is what currently costs the time.

**Phase 1 step 5 is next:** running the world once and each player's part separately. Before the code split itself, it needs a list of which of the main loop's per-frame calls are world and which are per player. I'll start that list from the 13 KB of per-player memory and the 23 functions above, unless you'd rather go a different way.
