## Claude

# Phase 1 step 5 in detail: running the world once

## Goal

Each frame, the world update runs once. Then, for each player, only the code that produces that player's view and status runs, with that player's ~13 KB of memory swapped in. Today, each player's whole 387 KB is copied in and out and the whole frame runs four times.

## Why the split is safe

The link cable carries only inputs (step 2), and four real GBAs stay in sync for a whole stage. So **nothing that differs between players can ever feed back into the world**. If one player's camera or HUD changed an enemy or the random number generator, the real GBAs would drift apart. The game is built so they don't, and that gives two rules:

- The bytes that differ between players (the ~13 KB from step 3) are the per-player state. Everything else is the shared world.
- Code that writes only per-player bytes is the "view" part, and it can run once per player after the world has updated.

So the work is mostly *finding* which code is the view part, not redesigning the game.

## What the frame looks like now

The game's main loop ([main.c](src/main.c)), once per frame:

| Call | What it is | World or player |
|---|---|---|
| `rom2_read_keys` | read the buttons | per player (each GBA's own pad) |
| `sub_0800C54C` | link: take the packet with everyone's keys | goes away (inputs come from a shared array) |
| `sub_08036864` | link state machine | goes away or becomes trivial |
| `gUnknown_0842731C[gMainState]()` | the game itself: entities, rooms, menus | **mixed**: world update plus camera, HUD and "mine?" checks inside |
| `sub_080368A0` | send this frame's packet | goes away |
| `sub_0800D788`, `sub_0800C118`, `sub_0802C940`, `sub_0800B524` | after the game: likely sound, sprite list, video registers | roles not yet known; probably mostly per player |

The hard part is the middle row, where world and view code are interleaved.

## Sub-steps

**5a. Find who writes the per-player bytes.**
- Extend the new `mgba_run --reads` into a write watch over the 13 KB ranges from step 3.
- Replay session 1 with it. The result is the list of functions that write per-player state, with their callers. That list is the view code.
- Also run step 3's memory diff at more points in session 1 (other rooms, menus, the end of the stage), so the 13 KB list is complete.

**5b. Sort every per-player function into one of three kinds.**
- **View only:** camera, background map streaming, sprite list, HUD, text boxes, the player's own sound. These move into the per-player pass.
- **World code with a "mine?" check inside:** for example `sub_08042DB0` sets an entity flag when the entity is the local player's Link. The check either moves to the per-player pass (if the flag only affects drawing) or the flag becomes per player.
- **Per-player arrays already indexed by player number:** keys, the link buffer, player records (`gUnknown_03006A30[id]`). These are naturally shared: the world already holds all four, and only "which one is mine" is per player.

Phase 0 found about 23 functions. Each needs reading to pick its kind. Most are decompiled C, and five are still asm.

**5c. Build it under `FS_SHARED_WORLD` in the port.**
- One world memory block instead of four. Each player has a small overlay of its ~13 KB, which `ps2_tlb_select` swaps (about 13 KB instead of 387 KB).
- Frame:
  1. Player 0 runs the full frame as now: world plus player 0's view.
  2. For players 1–3: swap in their overlay, set the player number byte (0x03000414), and run only the view functions from 5b.
- Inputs: each player's keys go straight into the arrays the link would have filled (step 6). The link code is skipped.
- This keeps player 0's frame identical to today's, so a mistake shows up as a wrong screen for players 1–3, not a broken world.

**5d. Check (step 7).**
Run the 4-instance build and the shared build on the same inputs, and compare each frame:
- the world memory against instance 0;
- each player's 13 KB overlay against instance i;
- each screen pixel for pixel. The GS readback check already does this.

The first mismatch names the byte, and `--reads` or the write watch finds the code.

## Risks

- **View code hidden inside the entity update.** If a "mine?" branch sits deep in an entity's update and only changes drawing, 5c has to call just that part per player. This is the main unknown; 5a will show how much of it there is.
- **The per-player pass doing world work twice.** If a function on the view list also writes world bytes, running it again for players 1–3 would update the world twice. The write watch from 5a flags any function that writes both kinds of bytes.
- **Coverage.** Session 1 covers one stage. Other stages, bosses, the shop and results may have view code it doesn't reach.

## Cost estimate

- **5a and the extra memory diffs:** about a session.
- **5b:** about a session, depending on how many functions turn up.
- **5c and 5d:** two to three sessions, mostly checking mismatches.

The first measurable result: switch cost falls from about 0.9M to roughly 0.05M cycles per player. That alone would bring 4 players under the 60 fps budget, going by the step 1 numbers.

Shall I start with 5a?

Each player's map around their own camera lives there. That fits the Step 30 wide-view result: the background repeats every 256 pixels and the area below line 160 holds stale tiles, because the game only fills a 32-tile ring around the GBA-sized view. Widening the view means changing the code that fills these buffers.

**2. Step 5a would find that code.** The planned write watch over the per-player bytes lists every function that writes them: camera, map streaming, sprite list, HUD. If it holds, the renderer could draw backgrounds for any viewport size straight from the room data, rather than from the game's 32-tile ring in VRAM. That would avoid rewriting the map streaming. Sprites and culling would still need game-side changes.

**4. The wide view's speed problem is mostly solved.** Wide 2-player drawing with the software renderer cost about 19M cycles a frame (about 12 fps). The GS renderer draws a 240x160 screen for about 0.6M, and its cost grows with the number of tiles, not pixels. A 320x240 view is about twice the tiles, so roughly 1.2M per screen. The GS renderer doesn't support the wide view yet; that's a contained change.

Both answers are yes. The whole room sits in memory every player shares, and the DSi widened the view by editing the GBA's own background-drawing routine. Committed as `b0c529f`, with walkthrough Step 39 and a new "Wider view" section in the Planning Doc; `make compare` reports OK.

**1. The whole room is in shared memory.** I checked the memory dumps from a 2-player stage frame:
- Both map layers cover the full stage: 63x63 blocks of 16x16 pixels, 1008x1008 pixels. Both are identical for the two players.
- Drawn from the dump with the tiles and palettes already loaded, the whole stage comes out complete (attached image). Each GBA only ever shows 240x160 of it.
- There's also a ready-made tile map of the whole room (128x128 tiles at 0x02016D90), complete and shared. A second one for the other layer, at 0x020231D0, isn't usable: outside the room it overlaps other data.

**2. How the game draws the background, and what the DSi changed.**
- `sub_08008ED8` is Four Swords' equivalent of Minish Cap's `UpdateScrollVram`. It runs an ARM routine, `sub_08008FA4`, that copies a 32x24-tile window of the room tile map into the 32x32 background map the GBA displays. So the GBA redraws 256x192 at a time.
- The DSi code has a copy of the same routine at 0x0207F7A0, with these changes:

| | GBA | DSi |
|---|---|---|
| Background map | 32 tiles wide (256 px) | 64 tiles wide (512 px), two map blocks |
| Rows redrawn | 24 | 32 |
| Tiles per row | 32 | 64 |
| One-tile margin around the view | yes | removed |
| Source | room tile map | the same room tile map |

  Together with the camera centred on 128/96 (found earlier), that's the DSi's widening. The source data is unchanged; only the copy got wider.

**What this means for the PS2's wider view.** There are two routes:
- **Do what the DSi did:** a 64x32 background map, a wider redraw, and wider row/column updates while scrolling. The GBA's video hardware supports that map size too. It covers views up to about 320x240, not 640 wide.
- **Draw from the room data in the PS2 renderer:** the backgrounds are drawn straight from the shared room data at any size, and the game's background map is left alone. This is the only option for the 640x240 two-player view.

**Not yet read in the DSi code:**
- the row/column scroll updates;
- the camera's edge limits;
- the culling that hides off-screen sprites;
- the HUD layout for the bigger screen.

Those are the next things to look at whenever the wider view comes back.

## Claude

# Wide view, option 2: drawing the backgrounds from the room data

The renderer stops relying on the game's 32-tile background map and draws the room itself, straight from the shared room data, at whatever size the view is. Backgrounds need almost no game changes. Sprites, the camera and the HUD do.

## What the renderer needs each frame

The camera position is in `gUnknown_03000450`, which is Four Swords' version of Minish Cap's room-controls struct. The GBA's own redraw routine reads these fields:

| Fields | Meaning |
|---|---|
| +0x18 / +0x1A | room origin |
| +0x1C / +0x1E | room size |
| +0x20 / +0x22 | camera x / y |

Together with the room data from Step 39, the renderer can draw any rectangle of the room.

## Steps, in order

**1. Backgrounds from the room data.** GS renderer only; no game changes.
- Draw the two room layers from the 63x63 metatile layers. Each metatile is four tile entries from the layer's metatile table, using the tiles already in video memory. I'd use the metatile layers for both layers, because the second layer's room-wide tile map isn't usable.
- Place the view so the GBA's 240x160 sits in its centre: view origin = camera − (W−240)/2, (H−160)/2.
- Draw only in scenes where the room layers are in use (a stage). Menus, the lobby and Choose a Stage keep today's 240x160 drawing, centred. To tell which background is a room layer, I'd match its map address against the ones the game's redraw writes to. That's a small check to work out.
- **Check:** the centre 240x160 of each wide frame must match the GBA's own frame pixel for pixel. The wide build already writes those comparison images.
- **Risk:** live tile changes (cut grass, switches). Minish Cap writes those into the layer data too, but I'll confirm it in a replay.

**2. Sprites.** This needs the game's sprite code. The game only puts on-screen sprites into its sprite list, by its own 240x160 culling, and the list's 9-bit x coordinate can't address 640 pixels anyway.
- Find the code that builds the sprite list and does the culling, using the write watch from the shared-world plan (step 5a) on the sprite buffer.
- In the PS2 build, widen the culling bounds and write a port-side sprite list with 16-bit coordinates. The renderer reads that list.

  Enemies and objects off a player's screen are still simulated, because the world is the same on every GBA. Only drawing is culled, so nothing else changes there.
- **Check:** within the centre 240x160, sprites must still match the GBA exactly.

**3. Camera.** The game centres on the player at 120/80 and stops at the room edges for a 240x160 screen. With step 1's centred offset, the view near an edge shows the area outside the room, drawn as the backdrop. That's acceptable at first. The proper fix is the DSi's: centre on half the view size and clamp with the bigger size. The camera is per-player state, so changing it can't desync the world (Phase 0 step 2).

**4. HUD.** The HUD layer is laid out for 240x160. It would first be drawn as-is in a 240-wide strip at the top centre; it's at the top, left to right. Spreading it to the corners (hearts left, rupees right) is a later rewrite of the HUD drawing.

**5. Windows and fades.** Fades cover the whole view. Window 0, used in the stage wipe, gets its coordinates offset into the wide view, with the area outside the 240x160 treated as outside the window.

## Sizes and cost

| Players | View per player |
|---|---|
| 1 | 320x240 |
| 2 | 640x240 each, stacked |
| 3–4 | 320x240 each, 2x2 grid |

On the GS, cost grows with the number of tiles. 640x240 is about 4.5 times the tiles of 240x160, roughly 1.5–2.5M cycles for two screens, if the tile-graphics upload is shared once the world is shared. That's affordable once the memory-switch cost is dealt with.

| 1 | about 1 | correct backgrounds in the whole wide view |
| 2 | 1–2 | depends on how readable the sprite code is (decompiled C or asm) |
| 3–5 | about 1 together | |

Step 2 overlaps with the shared-world plan's step 5a, since both need the same write watch.

Committed as `7651fda` (plus two small Makefile fixes); walkthrough Step 40 and the Planning Doc are updated, and `make compare` reports OK. The attached image shows both players' views at two stage frames.

**How it works**
- Before writing renderer code, I worked out the mapping on the memory dumps:
  - BG2 shows the room's top layer and BG1 its bottom layer.
  - Screen pixel x shows room pixel (camera − room origin) + x, and the scroll registers equal that value modulo 512.
  - All 651 visible tiles of both layers matched the room data, for both players' cameras.
- The renderer:
  - **Placement:** it draws the GBA picture in the middle of the view and fills the rest of the view with the room from its data.
  - **Self-check every frame:** before using the room data, it checks that the GBA screen's 31x21 tiles equal it. If they don't (menus, the lobby, a room change), that frame is drawn the old way, with repeating tiles.
  - **GBA-sized parts:** the HUD and sprites stay inside the GBA screen. The backdrop, fades and the window mask cover the whole view.
- Build with `make -f Makefile.ps2 WIDE_VIEW=1 GS_RENDER=1`. The wide view still defaults to the software renderer.

**Results (2-player replay)**
- All 34 check frames per screen, lobby to stage, match the software renderer's GBA picture exactly in the middle 240x160.
- No TLB misses.
- In the stage, the room continues to both sides with no repeating. The sand outside the cliffs is the game's separate background layer (BG3), which repeats as before.
- The normal 240x160 GS build is unchanged: 34 of 34 identical, 1.2M cycles.

**Limits**
- **Speed:** two 640x240 views take 3.35M EE cycles to draw. With the game's 1.84M that's over the 4.9M budget, so the wide 2-player view runs below 60 fps for now.
- **Still GBA-sized:**
  - Sprites: only what the game puts on its own screen gets drawn. Enemies or other Links just outside the middle 240x160 are missing.
  - The camera is still centred for 240x160.
  - The HUD sits in the middle strip.
  - The stage wipe (window 0) still uses the GBA screen's coordinates.

Why is GS memory tight? Is there anything we can do to free up RAM? My hope was eventually to have 9 screens drawing on a 1280x720 canvas

## Claude

# GS memory, and what 9 screens on 1280x720 would need

## Why it's tight

The GS has 4 MB of its own memory. For the vertical split:

| Use | Size |
|---|---|
| Displayed frame, 640x480 at 32-bit colour, double-buffered (one shown while the next is drawn) | 2 × 1.2 MB = 2.4 MB |
| One render target per player (each screen is drawn there, then copied into the frame), 320x480 at 32-bit | 2 × 0.6 MB = 1.2 MB |
| Tile graphics texture and palettes | 0.14 MB |
| **Total** | **≈ 3.75 MB of 4 MB** |

## What frees it

**1. Draw each screen straight into the frame.** The per-player render targets only exist because the first version copied a finished picture onto the screen. The renderer can instead draw each player's view directly at its spot in the frame, clipped to its rectangle. That saves the whole 1.2 MB, and the memory needed no longer grows with the number of players.

The window mask and the blend flag would then live in the frame's alpha instead of the target's. The pixel check would read the screen's rectangle from the frame.

**2. 16-bit colour instead of 32-bit.** The GBA only has 15-bit colour (5 bits per channel), so a 16-bit frame (5:5:5 plus 1 bit of alpha) loses no colour at all. That halves the frame buffers.

The 1 alpha bit is enough: the window mask and the blending flag each need one bit, and the renderer never uses both at once. While blending, the window is done with clipping rectangles instead. Blending and fades would then round to 5 bits, which is how the GBA itself does it, so it may even match mGBA more closely.

The texture and palettes are already shared: one copy, reused for each screen in turn.

## 1280x720 with 9 screens

With both changes:

| Use | Size |
|---|---|
| 1280x720 at 16-bit, double-buffered | 2 × 1.84 MB = 3.69 MB |
| Tiles and palettes | 0.14 MB |
| Per-player targets | none |
| **Total** | **≈ 3.8 MB** |

It fits, though barely, and it fits the same way for 1 or 9 players. A 3x3 grid on 1280x720 gives each player 426x240, a little wider than the 320x240 view. Today's 720p mode draws 640x720 and doubles it horizontally because of this memory limit. With 16-bit colour and no targets, true 1280x720 becomes possible.

## The bigger limits are on the EE side

GS memory is the easiest part of 9 players. The rest:

- **The game supports 4 players.** Its arrays are sized 4, player numbers are 2 bits wide, and the link protocol assumes 4. This is the Planning Doc's "more than 4 players" item.
- **Main RAM layout:** each game copy gets its own 1 MB block, and only 7 such blocks fit in the PS2's 32 MB as it's laid out now. With the shared world, a player needs about 13 KB, not 1 MB.
- **CPU:** copying memory between players costs about 0.9M cycles per player, so 9 players would spend 8M on copying alone, against a 4.9M frame budget. The shared world removes that.
- **Drawing:** each wide view costs roughly 1–1.5M EE cycles to draw today. Nine would need the tile upload done once per frame (it's per screen today) and cheaper per-tile drawing commands, or running at 30 fps.

So 9 players depends on the shared world (Phase 5) and the "more than 4 players" work. The two GS changes above are small and worth doing now. They free the memory for any layout, and drawing straight into the frame also removes a copy per screen. I'd estimate about a session for both, with the existing pixel checks proving nothing changed.

Want me to do them now?

## Claude

GS memory use is down from 3.75 MB to about 1.4 MB, and it no longer grows with the number of players or the view size. Committed as `52c93f0`, with walkthrough Step 42; `make compare` reports OK.

**The two changes:**
- **Screens draw straight into the frame.** Each screen is drawn at its place in the frame, scaled where needed (one player at 2x, the 16:9 squeeze). The per-player buffers and the copy step are gone.
- **16-bit frame.** The GBA's colours are 15-bit, so nothing is lost. The 1 spare alpha bit holds the window mask or the blending flag, which are never needed at the same time.

**GS memory now:**

| Use | Size |
|---|---|
| Frame, 640x480 16-bit, double-buffered | 2 × 0.6 MB |
| Tile graphics and palettes | 0.14 MB |
| **Total, any number of players** | **≈ 1.4 MB of 4 MB** |

A double-buffered 1280x720 frame (3.7 MB) would now fit, which is what the 9-screen layout needs.

**Checks (all with no TLB misses):**

| Build | Result |
|---|---|
| 2 players, 240x160 | 22 of 34 check frames identical; the other 12 are the fade/wipe frames, within one level |
| Vertical split, 320x480 | 14 of 34 identical, none more than one level off |
| 1 player at 2x (480p) | sharp and centred |

The check now compares at 5 bits per channel, the GBA's own precision. mGBA computes fades in 8-bit colour, so its values can't land exactly on the frame's 5-bit ones. The GBA hardware also rounds to 5 bits, so off by one in a fade isn't a sign the GS output is wrong.

**Side effects:**
- **16:9 mode:** it's no longer smoothed, so pixel columns there will vary slightly in width. Integer scales are unaffected.
- **Drawing cost:** two 240x160 screens went from 1.2M to 1.34M cycles per frame. A test with a 32-bit frame cost the same, so 16-bit colour isn't the cause. Most likely it's an accounting shift: the frame clear is still running when the next frame's drawing starts, so that wait now counts as drawing. I haven't confirmed this. A first version that scaled positions with floating point cost more; it now uses integers.

**What remains for 9 screens on 1280x720** is all on the EE side:
- the game itself supports only 4 players;
- each player's separate memory copy;
- the per-player memory switching, which the shared world would remove;
- drawing cost per screen.
